## v0.0.8 (October 2025): Protocol Integration and Multi-Model Support

The [v0.0.8 release](https://github.com/snap-stanford/Biomni/releases) landed in late October 2025 and brought several notable additions to the Biomni environment:

**Protocol.io Integration.** PR #251, merged by Serena Zhang, connected Biomni to [protocols.io](https://www.protocols.io) -- a widely-used platform for sharing and versioning experimental protocols. This allows the A1 agent to retrieve and reference structured, peer-reviewed protocols directly within its reasoning loop, rather than relying solely on static know-how documents. This is a meaningful step toward grounding agent actions in real lab practice.

**PyLabRobot Integration.** PR #210 by @serena2z introduced a bridge to [PyLabRobot](https://github.com/PyLabRobot/PyLabRobot), the open-source, hardware-agnostic Python library for liquid handling robots (Hamilton STAR, Tecan Freedom EVO, Opentrons OT-2, and more). Kexin Huang [announced on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/kexinhuang_announcing-biomni-pylabrobot-a-step-activity-7382082491798622209-KAH6): "Biomni x PyLabRobot -- a step toward an AI biologist that can think, design, and execute wet-lab experiments end-to-end." The collaboration involved Retro Biosciences and PyLabRobot creator Rick Wierenga. This marks the first time Biomni crossed the boundary from purely computational analysis into physical lab automation.

**GPT-5 Mini Support.** PR #246 by @mickaelleclercq added compatibility with GPT-5 mini, expanding the range of LLM providers users can plug into the agent framework. Combined with existing support for Claude, Gemini, Groq, Bedrock, Ollama, and Azure OpenAI, the agent now supports **eight LLM providers** out of the box.

**New Community Tools.** The release also absorbed contributions from multiple new contributors:
- @igor-sadalski added [State embeddings](https://github.com/snap-stanford/Biomni/pull/224) and [Transcripformer embeddings](https://github.com/snap-stanford/Biomni/pull/227) for gene representation
- @divyesh-htree fixed [Reactome API endpoints](https://github.com/snap-stanford/Biomni/pull/244) to use 2025-compatible URLs
- @zhanxw fixed package name casing issues

| Feature | PR | Contributor |
|---|---|---|
| PyLabRobot integration | #210 | @serena2z |
| Protocol.io integration | #251 | @serena2z |
| State embeddings tool | #224 | @igor-sadalski |
| Transcripformer embeddings tool | #227 | @igor-sadalski |
| GPT-5 mini support | #246 | @mickaelleclercq |
| Reactome API endpoint fix | #244 | @divyesh-htree |
| Package casing fix | #232 | @zhanxw |
| Eval improvements | #238 | @kexinhuang12345 |
| UI updates | #247 | @kexinhuang12345 |

---

## v0.0.7 (September 2025): The Community Expansion Release

The [v0.0.7 release](https://github.com/snap-stanford/Biomni/releases) was arguably the most contributor-heavy cycle to date. It introduced 25+ merged PRs and welcomed five first-time contributors.

**Key highlights:**

- **10 SOTA cell-type transfer algorithms** (PR #201, @igor-sadalski) -- a substantial addition for single-cell analysis workflows.
- **Gene name conversion across species** (PR #204) and **ESM embeddings from Ensembl gene IDs** (PR #205), also from @igor-sadalski.
- **Glycoengineering tools** (PR #212, @shantanusharma) for glycobiology workflows.
- **Bioimaging tools** (PR #207, @MintaYLu) covering pre-processing, segmentation, and registration -- directly relevant to the later Western Blot ROI detection work.
- **PDF conversation export** (PR #217, @igor-sadalski) enabling researchers to save agent execution traces as PDF reports for documentation and reproducibility.
- **Synapse data integration** (PR #173, @anngvu) for searching and downloading datasets from the Synapse platform.
- **Lazyslide support** (PR #156, @ryanDing26) for whole-slide image analysis.
- **Commercial mode configuration** (PR #200, @lxasqjc) for license-aware data filtering.
- **MCP tool parameter parsing fix** (PR #181, @Edison-A-N) addressing a structural bug in how auto-discovered MCP tools mapped required vs optional parameters.

---

## Post-Release Development (November 2025 - January 2026)

After the v0.0.8 tag, development continued on `main` with several impactful merges:

### Know-How Library Expansion

In early November, Yuanhao Qu added an [sgRNA Design know-how document](https://github.com/snap-stanford/Biomni/commit/e875ed42f89892f67d0ba8bd03a1f37729851725) describing a three-tiered approach to guide RNA design. This was followed by additional resource documents and minor fixes from Kexin Huang across the [know_how branch](https://github.com/snap-stanford/Biomni/pull/252).

### Protocol Database: Addgene and Thermo Fisher

Serena Zhang contributed a [protocol database expansion](https://github.com/snap-stanford/Biomni/commit/6603b4aa43694d2a2eb8565c484c16264dc68daf) incorporating protocols from [Addgene](https://www.addgene.org) and Thermo Fisher Scientific. This was merged in [PR #259](https://github.com/snap-stanford/Biomni/pull/259) on January 15, 2026, adding curated wet-lab protocol references directly into the agent's retrieval pipeline.

### Western Blot ROI Detection Tools

Contributor @nevergreendd added two new bioimaging tools in December 2025:
- `analyze_pixel_distribution` -- analyzes pixel intensity distributions across Western blot images
- `find_roi_from_image` -- detects regions of interest from blot images

These were merged via [PR #266](https://github.com/snap-stanford/Biomni/pull/266). This work complements the broader bioimaging toolset introduced in v0.0.7 and demonstrates how community contributors are filling domain-specific gaps.

### Gradio Version Compatibility Fix

Andrew Su (from the [Scripps Research Institute team](https://github.com/andrewsu)) identified and fixed a breaking change: Gradio 6.0 removed the `type="messages"` parameter from `Chatbot.__init__()`. The [fix in PR #268](https://github.com/snap-stanford/Biomni/pull/268) constrained the Gradio dependency to `>=5.0,<6.0` in `pyproject.toml` and updated the README installation instructions. As Andrew noted in the commit: "Users can now install with `pip install 'biomni[gradio]'` or manually with `pip install 'gradio>=5.0,<6.0'`."

### Pre-commit CI Housekeeping

The [pre-commit.ci bot](https://pre-commit.ci) kept linting tools current: biomejs/pre-commit was updated from v2.3.1 to v2.3.10, and ruff-pre-commit from v0.14.2 to v0.14.11, both via [PR #253](https://github.com/snap-stanford/Biomni/pull/253).

---

## The Biomni-R0 Reasoning Model

While not a code update per se, the release of [Biomni-R0-32B-Preview](https://huggingface.co/biomni/Biomni-R0-32B-Preview) on Hugging Face in September 2025 is the single most impactful recent event for the project. Announced by [Jure Leskovec on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/leskovec_biomni-r0-32b-preview-is-now-open-weight-activity-7384241679408631826-qsRe) as "beating GPT-5 and Claude Sonnet 4," the model is built on Qwen-32B and trained with end-to-end reinforcement learning using the Biomni-E1 environment.

The [technical report](https://biomni.stanford.edu/blog/biomni-r0-technical-report) describes a two-phase pipeline: supervised fine-tuning on high-quality Claude trajectories (rejection-sampled), followed by RL optimizing for both correctness and structured output formatting. Results on [Biomni-Eval1](https://huggingface.co/datasets/biomni/Eval1) are striking:

| Model | Eval1 Score | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Biomni-R0-32B | 0.669 | Best on 7/10 tasks |
| Biomni-R0-8B | 0.588 | Outperforms Claude 4 Sonnet & GPT-5 |
| Qwen-32B (base) | 0.346 | 2x improvement after RL |
| Claude 4 Sonnet | Lower | Best on 1/10 tasks |
| GPT-5 | Lower | Best on 2/10 tasks |

The model can be served locally via SGLang and plugged into the A1 agent as a reasoning backend while keeping database queries on a separate API provider -- a hybrid architecture that the project explicitly recommends. The v0.0.8 release included README updates from @RyanLi0802 to document this workflow.

---

## Forward-Looking: Community Requests and Biomni-E2

The [issues tracker](https://github.com/snap-stanford/Biomni/issues) reveals an active community pushing the project in several directions:

**Imaging tool requests.** The [Cellpose integration proposal](https://github.com/snap-stanford/Biomni/issues/202) seeks to incorporate the [MouseLand/cellpose](https://github.com/MouseLand/cellpose) cell and nucleus segmentation model, which would complement the existing bioimaging toolset and the new Western Blot ROI detection capabilities.

**LLM provider flexibility.** The [OpenRouter integration request](https://github.com/snap-stanford/Biomni/issues/90) proposes adding OpenRouter as a unified gateway to 50+ LLM providers. The contributor even drafted a code snippet showing how it could work with the existing `source`/`base_url` routing logic.

**Reliability concerns.** Multiple issues -- [R0 example stuck in loop](https://github.com/snap-stanford/Biomni/issues/257), [stuck loops and parsing errors](https://github.com/snap-stanford/Biomni/issues/272), and [Claude Sonnet 4.6 prefill error](https://github.com/snap-stanford/Biomni/issues/284) -- highlight a recurring structural challenge: the agent's response parser expects specific tag formats (`<think`, `<execute`, `<solution>`), and different LLMs produce different output patterns. One user reported that GLM-4.7 responds with `reasoning` instead of `think`, causing the identifier to loop indefinitely. These are real friction points for anyone using non-default LLM backends.

**Environment setup.** The [setup.sh dependency issue](https://github.com/snap-stanford/Biomni/issues/283) with pystan requiring `Cython>=0.22` and numpy, and the [outdated README time estimates](https://github.com/snap-stanford/Biomni/issues/267) for setup on Apple Silicon, suggest that documentation could use a refresh.

**RAG safety framework.** A particularly thoughtful [feature request](https://github.com/snap-stanford/Biomni/issues/282) proposes integrating a structured RAG failure taxonomy (the WFGY ProblemMap, cited by Harvard MIMS Lab and others) into Biomni's documentation. This would give users a systematic way to classify and debug retrieval failures -- a clear need for a system that stitches together 59 databases.

**The Biomni-E2 call to action.** The README prominently features a call for contributors to help build [Biomni-E2](https://github.com/snap-stanford/Biomni#-call-for-contributors-help-build-biomni-e2) -- a next-generation environment "developed with and for the community." Contributors with 10+ significant tool integrations are offered co-authorship on the upcoming E2 paper. Given the velocity of community contributions in v0.0.7 and v0.0.8, this is an ambitious but plausible target.

---

## Summary: What to Watch

The trajectory is clear: Biomni is moving from a computational-only agent toward a **full-stack AI research assistant** that can reason, retrieve, analyze images, and increasingly, orchestrate physical lab equipment. The most significant recent shifts are:

1. **Wet-lab bridge via PyLabRobot** -- the agent can now generate protocols that run on real liquid handling robots.
2. **Domain-specific vision tools** -- Western Blot ROI detection and bioimaging preprocessing indicate a push into image analysis.
3. **Protocol grounding** -- Protocol.io and Addgene/Thermo protocol databases give the agent structured, real-world experimental references.
4. **Custom reasoning model** -- Biomni-R0-32B achieves expert-level biomedical reasoning through RL, and can serve as a local, cost-effective alternative to frontier API models.
5. **Growing contributor velocity** -- v0.0.7 alone welcomed five new contributors; the codebase is absorbing external expertise at an accelerating rate.

For developers, the practical takeaway is straightforward: if you are building biomedical workflows that involve multi-step reasoning across heterogeneous tools and databases, Biomni is worth watching closely. But if you need rock-solid reliability with non-standard LLM backends, you should expect to do some parser patching. The project is transparent about this -- the README itself notes that "many current tools are not optimized" and explicitly welcomes fixes.

# Biomni-R0 Reasoning Model



**Biomni-R0** is the first open-weight reasoning model trained specifically for biomedical agentic tasks. Rather than slapping a generic LLM into a bio-agent scaffold and hoping for the best, the Biomni team -- in collaboration with UC Berkeley's SkyRL group -- took a fundamentally different approach: they trained the model *end-to-end* inside the Biomni-E1 environment using reinforcement learning. The result is a domain-specialized model that turns out to be more than a curiosity -- it outperforms frontier closed-source models on the team's own benchmark across most tasks, and does so at 32 billion parameters.

This page covers the model's design, training, deployment, and the practical realities of using it.

---

## Why a Dedicated Reasoning Model?

The Biomni agent framework (covered in the [Architecture Overview](8-architecture-overview) and [A1 Agent Core Class](9-a1-agent-core-class)) is LLM-agnostic by design. You can plug in Claude, GPT-4, or any OpenAI-compatible model as the reasoning engine. But here is the structural problem: a general-purpose model has never *seen* biomedical tool calls, code execution in a bioinformatics environment, or the structured think-execute-solution loop that Biomni relies on during training. As [Kexin Huang noted on X](https://x.com/KexinHuang5/status/1962916295055442005), R0 is "nearly 2x stronger than its open-source base" and ">10% better than frontier closed-source models."

The premise is straightforward -- if you want a model that reasons well *within* a specific environment, you should train it *inside* that environment. Biomni-R0 is that bet.

---

## Model Lineup

Biomni-R0 comes in two sizes, both built on Qwen as the base architecture:

| Variant | Parameters | Base Model | Status |
|---------|-----------|------------|--------|
| Biomni-R0-8B | ~8B | Qwen2.5-8B (implied) | Referenced in technical report; not yet publicly released |
| **Biomni-R0-32B-Preview** | ~32B | Qwen-32B | Available on [HuggingFace](https://huggingface.co/biomni/Biomni-R0-32B-Preview) |

The publicly available **Biomni-R0-32B-Preview** is a research preview. The weights are hosted at `biomni/Biomni-R0-32B-Preview` on HuggingFace, and quantized GGUF variants are also available through community contributors like [mradermacher](https://huggingface.co/mradermacher/Biomni-R0-32B-Preview-GGUF).

---

## Training Methodology

The training pipeline is described in the [technical report](https://biomni.stanford.edu/blog/biomni-r0-technical-report) and represents a collaboration between Stanford's Biomni team (Ryan Li, Kexin Huang, Yuanhao Qu, Jure Leskovec) and UC Berkeley's [SkyRL](https://sky.cs.berkeley.edu/project/skyrl) group (Shiyi Cao et al.). The process follows a two-phase approach:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Qwen-32B Base Model] --> B[Phase 1: Supervised Fine-Tuning]
    B --> C[Claude-4 Sonnet trajectories sampled with rejection sampling]
    C --> D[Bootstrapped model with structured reasoning format]
    D --> E[Phase 2: Reinforcement Learning via SkyRL]
    E --> F{Dual Reward Structure}
    F --> G[Correctness Reward - e.g., right gene, correct diagnosis]
    F --> H[Formatting Reward - proper think/execute/solution tags]
    G --> I[Biomni-R0-32B-Preview]
    H --> I
    style I fill:#2563eb,color:#fff
```

### Phase 1: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)

The base Qwen-32B model was first fine-tuned on high-quality trajectories sampled from Claude-4 Sonnet using **rejection sampling**. The purpose was not to make the model a Claude clone -- it was to bootstrap it into following the structured reasoning format that the Biomni-E1 environment expects: thinking blocks, executable code blocks, and solution blocks.

### Phase 2: Reinforcement Learning

This is where the interesting work happens. Using [SkyRL](https://github.com/NovaSky-AI/SkyRL), Berkeley's RL training infrastructure for multi-turn tool-use LLMs, the team optimized the model with two reward signals:

1. **Correctness reward**: Does the agent produce the right biological answer? (e.g., identifying the correct causal gene, making the right diagnosis)
2. **Formatting reward**: Does the agent output properly structured responses with the expected XML-like tags?

The RL training was done *within the Biomni-E1 environment*, meaning the model received rewards based on actual tool execution results, database queries, and multi-turn interactions -- not just text prediction quality.

### Key Engineering Decisions

Several infrastructure choices made this training pipeline feasible:

- **Asynchronous rollout scheduling**: Environment execution (tool calls, database queries) was decoupled from model inference. This prevented GPU starvation during long-running tool executions and kept training throughput reasonable.
- **Extended context window**: The context length was expanded to 64k tokens (via YaRN RoPE scaling), enabling the model to maintain coherent reasoning across long multi-step biomedical workflows.
- **Longer reasoning traces correlated with better performance**: The RL-trained models consistently produced lengthier, more structured responses, and this correlated strongly with better task outcomes -- suggesting that the model learned that *depth of reasoning* matters in biomedicine.

---

## Benchmark Results

Biomni-R0 was evaluated on [Biomni-Eval1](7-biomni-eval1-benchmark-results), a benchmark of 433 instances across 10 biomedical reasoning tasks. The headline numbers, as reported in the technical report and summarized by [third-party coverage](https://metaailabs.com/biomni-r0-new-agentic-llms-trained-end-to-end-with-multi-turn-reinforcement-learning-for-expert-level-intelligence-in-biomedical-research):

| Model | Aggregate Score | Notes |
|-------|----------------|-------|
| Qwen-32B (base) | 0.346 | No biomedical RL training |
| **Biomni-R0-8B** | **0.588** | 8B model with RL; outperforms Claude 4 Sonnet and GPT-5 |
| **Biomni-R0-32B** | **0.669** | Top performer on 7 out of 10 tasks |
| Claude 4 Sonnet | ~0.56 | Frontier closed-source model |
| GPT-5 | ~0.56 | Frontier closed-source model; top on 2 tasks |

**Most striking individual results:**

- **Rare disease diagnosis**: Biomni-R0-32B scored **0.67**, compared to Qwen-32B's **0.03** -- a **20x improvement**. This is arguably the strongest signal that domain-specific RL training matters.
- **GWAS variant prioritization**: Score jumped from **0.16** (base) to **0.74** (R0-32B).
- GPT-5 led on 2 tasks, Claude 4 on 1 task.

The fact that an 8B parameter model (R0-8B) outperforms frontier closed-source models is notable and speaks to the efficiency of the training methodology. But keep in mind: this is self-reported on their own benchmark, and independent replication would be valuable.

---

## Deployment and Serving

Biomni-R0 is served via [SGLang](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang), an efficient serving framework that provides an OpenAI-compatible API. This is important because it means the Biomni agent can talk to R0 through the same interface it uses for Claude or GPT -- just pointed at a local endpoint.

### Hardware Requirements

Per the [HuggingFace model card](https://huggingface.co/biomni/Biomni-R0-32B-Preview):

- **Minimum**: 2 GPUs with 80GB VRAM (tensor parallelism `--tp 2`)
- **Alternative**: 4 GPUs with 40GB VRAM (`--tp 4`)

This is not a model you run on a consumer GPU. If you lack this hardware, quantized GGUF versions (down to ~7.4GB at IQ1_S) are available for inference via llama.cpp, though with expected quality degradation.

### Launch Command

```bash
python -m sglang.launch_server \
    --model-path biomni/Biomni-R0-32B-Preview \
    --port 30000 \
    --host 0.0.0.0 \
    --mem-fraction-static 0.8 \
    --tp 2 \
    --trust-remote-code \
    --json-model-override-args '{
        "rope_scaling": {
            "rope_type": "yarn",
            "factor": 1.0,
            "original_max_position_embeddings": 32768
        },
        "max_position_embeddings": 131072
    }'
```

**RoPE scaling notes**: The model's native context is 32,768 tokens. The configuration above extends it to 131,072 (128k) using YaRN scaling with `factor=1.0`. If your tasks produce even longer reasoning traces, you can increase the factor up to `4.0`, but the HuggingFace card warns that this **may degrade performance on shorter-trajectory tasks**. Tune accordingly.

### Wiring It Into the Agent

The recommended pattern is a **hybrid setup**: use Biomni-R0 for agent reasoning, but keep a capable API model (Claude, GPT) for database queries and retrieval tasks. This separation is important because R0, while excellent at reasoning, is a smaller model and may struggle with the nuances of complex retrieval prompts.

```python
from biomni.config import default_config
from biomni.agent import A1

# Database queries use a capable API model
default_config.llm = "claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022"
default_config.source = "Anthropic"

# Agent reasoning uses local Biomni-R0
agent = A1(
    llm="biomni/Biomni-R0-32B-Preview",
    source="Custom",
    base_url="http://localhost:30000/v1",
    api_key="EMPTY",
)

agent.go("Plan a CRISPR screen to identify genes regulating T cell exhaustion")
```

This configuration pattern is also documented in the [Configuration Reference](21-configuration-reference).

---

## Known Issues and Practical Considerations

Despite the impressive benchmark numbers, the community has reported several real-world friction points. If you are planning to deploy Biomni-R0 in production, these are worth understanding upfront.

### Parsing Errors and Infinite Loops

The most frequently reported issue class involves the model failing to produce the expected structured tags, causing the agent to enter an infinite retry loop. This was reported in [issue #257](https://github.com/snap-stanford/Biomni/issues/257) and discussed at length in [issue #272](https://github.com/snap-stanford/Biomni/issues/272).

The core problem: the agent's response parser expects specific tags (`<think reasoning="...">`, `<execute>`, `<solution>`). When R0 (or any substitute model) fails to emit these tags, the agent injects a corrective prompt and re-requests the response. If the model consistently fails to format correctly, you get an infinite loop of retries:

```
parsing error...
Each response must include thinking process followed by either <execute> or <solution> tag.
parsing error...
Each response must include thinking process followed by either <execute> or <solution> tag.
...
```

**Contributing factors:**

- **Non-standard response patterns**: As one user documented in [issue #272](https://github.com/snap-stanford/Biomni/issues/272), different LLMs use different reasoning keywords. GLM-4.7, for example, uses "reasoning" where the prompt expects "think", causing the identifier to miss the tag entirely.
- **R0's self-correction limits**: In hybrid mode (R0 for reasoning, API model as fallback), R0 may attempt to fix its own errors but reuse the same failing code repeatedly, creating a different kind of loop.
- **Newer model incompatibilities**: [Issue #284](https://github.com/snap-stanford/Biomni/issues/284) reports that Claude Sonnet 4.6 removed support for assistant message prefill, causing a 400 error when used as the agent LLM.

### Missing Internal Module

[Issue #285](https://github.com/snap-stanford/Biomni/issues/285) reports that `biomni.agent.base_agent` -- which `PaperTaskExtractor` inherits from -- is missing from the installed package. This suggests a packaging or export issue in the current release that the team has not yet addressed.

### Offline and Resource-Constrained Environments

Users trying to run Biomni-R0 in fully offline environments, as documented in the now-closed [issue #271](https://github.com/snap-stanford/Biomni/issues/271), encounter input length errors and connection failures. The model's large system prompt (37k+ tokens in some configurations) can exceed the default context limit, requiring `--allow-auto-truncate` at the cost of potential information loss.

### The Fundamental Tension

These issues point to a deeper architectural tension: the structured tag-based response format is simultaneously the mechanism that enables RL training and a source of fragility when models diverge from the expected pattern. The R0 model, having been trained specifically for this format, should in theory be the most reliable at producing it -- but in practice, deployment conditions (quantization, different serving frameworks, hardware constraints) can still cause deviations.

---

## How Biomni-R0 Fits Into the Ecosystem

Understanding R0's role requires seeing where it sits in the broader agent pipeline:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph "User Layer"
        U[Natural Language Query]
    end

    subgraph "Agent Layer (Biomni A1)"
        P[Retrieval-Augmented Planning]
        R[R0 or API Model<br/>Multi-step Reasoning]
    end

    subgraph "Execution Layer"
        T[Tool Execution<br/>150 tools / 59 DBs / 105 software]
        E[Code Interpreter]
    end

    subgraph "Knowledge Layer"
        K[Know-How Library]
        DL[Data Lake ~11GB]
    end

    U --> P
    P --> R
    R --> T
    R --> E
    P --> K
    P --> DL
    T --> R
    E --> R
    R --> U

    style R fill:#2563eb,color:#fff,stroke:#1d4ed8
```

R0 occupies the **reasoning slot** -- it is the model that decides *what to do next* given the current context. It does not replace the tool system, the data layer, or the retrieval mechanism. In practice, the most robust deployments use R0 for reasoning while delegating retrieval and database queries to more capable API models.

# Biomni-Eval1 Benchmark Results



## What Is Biomni-Eval1?

Biomni-Eval1 is the first standardized evaluation benchmark released alongside the Biomni agent, designed to measure **biological reasoning capabilities** across a genuinely heterogeneous set of tasks rather than narrow Q&A slices. As [Jure Leskovec announced on X](https://x.com/jure/status/1978470668732928310), the benchmark ships with **4,880 instances** (4,447 train + 433 validation) spanning **10 distinct biological reasoning tasks** -- everything from GWAS causal gene identification to rare disease diagnosis to CRISPR delivery method selection.

The dataset is hosted on Hugging Face at [biomni/Eval1](https://huggingface.co/datasets/biomni/Eval1) and is accessible programmatically through the `BiomniEval1` class bundled in the `biomni` pip package.

The full methodology and results are described in the [Biomni preprint on bioRxiv](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.05.30.656746v1) (also indexed on [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40501924/)).

---

## Task Breakdown

The 10 tasks in Eval1 cover a deliberately wide cross-section of biomedical reasoning -- from literature-driven database lookups to multi-step clinical inference. Here is the full distribution as documented on the [Hugging Face dataset card](https://huggingface.co/datasets/biomni/Eval1):

| Task | Train | Val | Total | Domain |
|------|-------|-----|-------|--------|
| `gwas_causal_gene_pharmaprojects` | 1,353 | 50 | 1,403 | Genetics / Genomics |
| `gwas_causal_gene_opentargets` | 680 | 50 | 730 | Genetics / Genomics |
| `gwas_causal_gene_gwas_catalog` | 512 | 50 | 562 | Genetics / Genomics |
| `lab_bench_seqqa` | 480 | 50 | 530 | Molecular Biology (Q&A) |
| `lab_bench_dbqa` | 416 | 50 | 466 | Molecular Biology (DB access) |
| `patient_gene_detection` | 400 | 50 | 450 | Clinical Genomics |
| `screen_gene_retrieval` | 278 | 50 | 328 | Functional Genomics |
| `gwas_variant_prioritization` | 172 | 43 | 215 | Genetics |
| `rare_disease_diagnosis` | 116 | 30 | 146 | Clinical Genomics |
| `crispr_delivery` | 40 | 10 | 50 | Synthetic Biology |
| **Total** | **4,447** | **433** | **4,880** | |

Validation splits are capped at 50 instances per task (or fewer if the task has fewer than 50 val instances), which means the held-out test set is small but curated for reliability.

### Task Categories at a Glance

```mermaid
graph TD
    A[Biomni-Eval1<br/>4,880 instances] --> B[Genetics / GWAS]
    A --> C[Molecular Biology<br/>LAB-Bench]
    A --> D[Clinical Genomics]
    A --> E[Functional Genomics]
    A --> F[Synthetic Biology]

    B --> B1[gwas_causal_gene_pharmaprojects<br/>1,403]
    B --> B2[gwas_causal_gene_opentargets<br/>730]
    B --> B3[gwas_causal_gene_gwas_catalog<br/>562]
    B --> B4[gwas_variant_prioritization<br/>215]

    C --> C1[lab_bench_seqqa<br/>530]
    C --> C2[lab_bench_dbqa<br/>466]

    D --> D1[patient_gene_detection<br/>450]
    D --> D2[rare_disease_diagnosis<br/>146]

    E --> E1[screen_gene_retrieval<br/>328]
    F --> F1[crispr_delivery<br/>50]
```

---

## Evaluation Methodology

Each task uses **binary scoring** -- the agent either gets the answer right (1.0) or wrong (0.0). But the validation logic is not uniform; it adapts to the expected answer format for each task type, as documented in the [evaluation source code](https://github.com/snap-stanford/Biomni/blob/main/biomni/eval/biomni_eval1.py):

| Task Name | Expected Answer Format | Validation Logic |
|-----------|----------------------|------------------|
| `gwas_causal_gene_*` | Gene symbol (e.g., `"BRCA1"`) | Case-insensitive exact match |
| `gwas_variant_prioritization` | Variant ID (e.g., `"rs1065852"`) | Exact match |
| `lab_bench_*` | Letter A-Z (e.g., `"C"`) | Case-insensitive exact match |
| `rare_disease_diagnosis` | JSON with `OMIM_ID` field | JSON parsing + OMIM_ID match |
| `crispr_delivery` | Letter a-f (e.g., `"e"`) | Case-insensitive exact match |
| `screen_gene_retrieval` | Gene symbol | Case-insensitive exact match |
| `patient_gene_detection` | JSON with `causal_gene` list | JSON parsing + set intersection (non-empty overlap) |

For JSON-based tasks (`rare_disease_diagnosis`, `patient_gene_detection`), the evaluator tries multiple parsing strategies -- standard `json.loads()`, then `ast.literal_eval()`, then falls back to 0.0 -- which is a pragmatic design choice even if it is somewhat lenient on formatting.

### What This Means for Developers

The binary reward structure makes it straightforward to track progress, but it also means the benchmark is **unforgiving of near-misses**. A gene symbol with a trailing space or a JSON missing a comma both score 0.0. This is by design -- in clinical genomics, you need the exact right gene or the exact right OMIM ID -- but developers should be aware that improving scores requires not just better reasoning but also robust answer formatting.

---

## Key Results from the Paper

The [Biomni preprint](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.05.30.656746v1) reports strong zero-shot generalization across the eight novel biomedical scenarios evaluated on Eval1, with Biomni outperforming baseline approaches including bare LLMs and ReAct+Code setups without the Biomni environment.

As noted in [Leskovec's launch announcement](https://x.com/jure/status/1928130906033975768), the headline claims include:

- **Human-level performance on LAB-Bench DbQA and SeqQA**, the two molecular biology Q&A tasks included in Eval1.
- **State-of-the-art results on Humanity's Last Exam (HLE)** biomedical subset -- a notably hard benchmark where, as [Stanford HAI's 2025 AI Index](https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-index/2025-ai-index-report/technical-performance) notes, the top system at the time scored only 8.80%.
- **Up to 402% relative performance gain** on real-world biomedical tasks compared to non-agent baselines (base LLM and ReAct+Code without the Biomni environment).

### Comparative Performance Landscape

While the paper's own internal numbers are the authoritative source, external evaluations provide useful context:

- **Edison Scientific's Edison Analysis** (the successor to FutureHouse's Finch) reports 70% accuracy on Eval1, explicitly surpassing both Biomni and Claude Code on that benchmark, according to their [product announcement](https://edisonscientific.com/articles/introducing-edison-analysis). This is a notable external data point -- it suggests Eval1 is being adopted as a cross-system comparison point beyond the original paper.
- **BioML-bench** ([bioRxiv preprint](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.09.01.673319v2)), an independent benchmarking effort evaluating biomedical AI agents on end-to-end ML tasks, includes Biomni as one of four tested agents. They found that biomedical specialization does not consistently confer advantages over generalist agents, and that "agents which employed more diverse ML strategies more often tended to score highest."

```mermaid
timeline
    title Eval1 Benchmark Timeline & External Adoption
    May 2025 : "Biomni preprint released on bioRxiv with Eval1 results"
    Jun 2025 : "Dataset published on Hugging Face (biomni/Eval1)"
    Jul 2025 : "Jure Leskovec announces Biomni-R0-32B-Preview with Eval1 on X"
    Sep 2025 : "BioML-bench independently evaluates Biomni on end-to-end ML tasks"
    Late 2025 : "Edison Scientific reports 70% accuracy on Eval1 with Edison Analysis"
```

---

## Running the Benchmark Yourself

The eval infrastructure is deliberately lightweight -- a single class, a single pip install. Here is the standard workflow, also documented in the [README](https://github.com/snap-stanford/Biomni):

```python
from biomni.eval import BiomniEval1

# Initialize -- downloads dataset from Hugging Face on first run
evaluator = BiomniEval1()

# Quick programmatic check
score = evaluator.evaluate('gwas_causal_gene_opentargets', 0, 'BRCA1')
print(score)  # 1.0 if correct, 0.0 if wrong
```

### End-to-End Agent Evaluation

The more interesting usage pattern wires the evaluator into the full agent loop:

```python
from biomni.eval import BiomniEval1
from biomni.agent import A1

evaluator = BiomniEval1()
agent = A1(path='./data', llm='claude-sonnet-4-20250514')

# Grab a benchmark instance
instance = evaluator.get_instance('rare_disease_diagnosis', 5)
print(f"Prompt: {instance['prompt']}")
print(f"Ground truth: {instance['answer']}")

# Run it through the agent
agent.go(instance['prompt'])

# Extract the answer from agent output and score it
extracted_answer = ...  # parse from agent.conversation_history
score = evaluator.evaluate('rare_disease_diagnosis', 5, extracted_answer)
```

### Batch Evaluation

For systematic benchmarking, the `batch_evaluate()` method handles multiple evaluations with per-instance error isolation -- a single failure returns 0.0 without aborting the batch:

```python
evaluations = [
    ('gwas_causal_gene_opentargets', 0, 'BRCA1'),
    ('gwas_causal_gene_opentargets', 1, 'TP53'),
    ('crispr_delivery', 0, 'e'),
    ('rare_disease_diagnosis', 0, '{"OMIM_ID": "154700"}'),
]
scores = evaluator.batch_evaluate(evaluations)
```

### Dataset Inspection

The `BiomniEval1` class also exposes introspection methods for understanding benchmark composition, useful when planning evaluation runs or selecting subsets:

```python
evaluator = BiomniEval1()

# List all task names
evaluator.list_tasks()
# ['crispr_delivery', 'gwas_causal_gene_genebass', ...]

# Get aggregate statistics
stats = evaluator.get_task_stats()
# {'total_instances': 433, 'train_instances': 346, 'val_instances': 87, ...}

# Per-task breakdown
evaluator.get_task_stats('crispr_delivery')
# {'total_instances': 50, 'train_instances': 40, 'val_instances': 10}
```

---

## Design Critique: Strengths and Gaps

### What Eval1 Does Well

**Genuine breadth.** Most biomedical agent benchmarks focus on a single modality -- either Q&A (like [LAB-Bench](https://github.com/Future-House/LAB-Bench)), coding, or retrieval. Eval1 spans gene prioritization, clinical diagnosis, protocol selection, and database Q&A. That is a much better proxy for what a "general-purpose biomedical agent" actually needs to do.

**Binary, unambiguous scoring.** The reward function is deterministic and inspectable. Gene symbols, variant IDs, and OMIM IDs have canonical forms. There is no fuzzy LLM-as-judge component, which means results are fully reproducible and resistant to prompt sensitivity.

**Tied to the environment.** Eval1 is not a disembodied Q&A benchmark. Tasks like `gwas_causal_gene_*` and `lab_bench_dbqa` implicitly require the agent to use the Biomni-E1 environment's tools and databases to find answers. This makes the benchmark a better test of the full agent pipeline (retrieval, planning, code execution, answer extraction) rather than just the LLM's parametric knowledge.

### Where Eval1 Falls Short

**Small validation set.** With only 433 validation instances across 10 tasks, statistical power is limited -- especially for `crispr_delivery` (10 val instances) and `rare_disease_diagnosis` (30). A single lucky or unlucky guess swings task-level accuracy by 3-10 percentage points. This matters when comparing systems that are close in performance.

**No partial credit.** The binary scoring is clean but harsh. On `patient_gene_detection`, if the ground truth is `["BRCA1", "TP53"]` and the agent returns `["ATM"]`, the set intersection is empty and the score is 0.0 -- even though `ATM` might be a plausible causal gene for that patient. There is no mechanism for awarding partial credit, which could mask meaningful differences between systems.

**Answer format fragility.** The benchmark penalizes formatting errors as harshly as reasoning errors. As multiple [GitHub issues](https://github.com/snap-stanford/Biomni/issues/257) have documented, the agent can sometimes enter parsing loops where it fails to produce properly structured output. In an eval context, this means you cannot always distinguish "the agent reasoned incorrectly" from "the agent reasoned correctly but formatted its answer wrong."

**Retrieval-heavy tasks may conflate environment quality with agent quality.** Several tasks (`gwas_causal_gene_*`, `lab_bench_dbqa`) are primarily exercises in querying the right database with the right parameters. Strong performance on these may reflect the quality of the integrated databases more than the agent's reasoning ability. External benchmarks like BioML-bench, which evaluate end-to-end ML pipelines, provide a complementary perspective.

---

## Relationship to Other Benchmarks

Eval1 occupies a specific niche in the biomedical agent benchmark landscape. It is worth understanding how it relates to other evaluation efforts:

| Benchmark | Focus | Eval Format | Relation to Eval1 |
|-----------|-------|-------------|-------------------|
| **Biomni-Eval1** | Multi-task biomedical reasoning | Binary exact match | This benchmark |
| [LAB-Bench](https://github.com/Future-House/LAB-Bench) | Molecular biology Q&A and DB access | Multiple choice + structured | Eval1 includes LAB-Bench DbQA and SeqQA subsets |
| [BioML-bench](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.09.01.673319v2) | End-to-end biomedical ML pipelines | Metric-based (AUROC, Spearman) | Complementary -- tests different skills |
| [Humanity's Last Exam](https://artificialanalysis.ai/evaluations/humanitys-last-exam) | Cross-domain expert-level reasoning | Multiple choice | Eval1 includes an HLE biomedical subset |
| [BetterBench](https://betterbench.stanford.edu) | Meta-evaluation of AI benchmarks | Quality criteria assessment | Framework for assessing benchmarks like Eval1 itself |

Edison Scientific's adoption of Eval1 as a comparison point in their [Edison Analysis announcement](https://edisonscientific.com/articles/introducing-edison-analysis) is a meaningful signal -- it suggests the benchmark is being recognized beyond its original paper as a shared evaluation standard.

---

## Practical Tips for Developers

1. **Start with the validation split.** The 433-instance val set is the intended test set. The training split (4,447 instances) is much larger and should be used for development and debugging, not for reporting final numbers.

2. **Watch for answer extraction.** The evaluator expects a clean string or JSON object. If your agent wraps its answer in markdown code blocks, natural language justification, or XML tags, you will need to parse those out before calling `evaluate()`. The [parsing loop issues](https://github.com/snap-stanford/Biomni/issues/257) reported by users are a real concern in eval contexts.

3. **Use `batch_evaluate()` for systematic runs.** It handles exceptions gracefully and returns a list of scores, making it straightforward to compute per-task and aggregate accuracy.

4. **Track per-task breakdowns, not just averages.** A high overall accuracy can mask weak performance on clinically important tasks like `rare_disease_diagnosis`. The `get_task_stats()` method makes this easy.

5. **Be aware of environment dependency.** Tasks that require database access need the full Biomni-E1 environment (including the ~11GB data lake). You can skip data lake loading for evaluation-only workflows by setting `expected_data_lake_files=[]` if you are only testing non-database tasks.

---

- **Paper:** [Biomni: A General-Purpose Biomedical AI Agent (bioRxiv)](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.05.30.656746v1)

# Architecture Overview



![Biomni Logo](https://github.com/snap-stanford/Biomni/blob/main/figs/biomni_logo.png?raw=true)

Biomni is a **code-agent framework** designed for autonomous biomedical problem-solving. Rather than wrapping API calls behind a chat interface, it places an LLM inside a stateful coding loop where the model plans, writes code, executes it against real data and tools, observes results, and iterates — all within a single conversational thread. This page maps the layered architecture that makes this possible, from configuration down to code execution, and shows how data flows through the system from your first prompt to a final answer.

## High-Level Architecture

The system follows a **five-layer architecture**: Configuration → Agent Core → Resource Management → Execution Engine → Evaluation. Each layer has a single responsibility and communicates through well-defined interfaces, making the system both extensible and auditable.

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph User["User Interface Layer"]
        G[Gradio Demo]
        API["Python API<br/>agent.go(prompt)"]
        GS["agent.go_stream(prompt)"]
    end

    subgraph Agent["Agent Core Layer"]
        A1["A1 Agent<br/>(biomni/agent/a1.py)"]
        REACT["ReAct Agent<br/>(biomni/agent/react.py)"]
        A1 -- "primary" --> A1
        REACT -- "alternative" --> REACT
    end

    subgraph Resources["Resource Management Layer"]
        TR["Tool Registry<br/>(tool/tool_registry.py)"]
        Ret["Tool Retriever<br/>(model/retriever.py)"]
        DL["Data Lake<br/>(env_desc.py)"]
        KH["Know-How Loader<br/>(know_how/loader.py)"]
    end

    subgraph Execution["Execution Engine"]
        PY["Python REPL<br/>(support_tools.py)"]
        R["R Code Runner<br/>(utils.py)"]
        BASH["Bash Executor<br/>(utils.py)"]
        MCP["MCP Client"]
    end

    subgraph Eval["Evaluation Layer"]
        BE1["BiomniEval1<br/>(eval/biomni_eval1.py)"]
        BT["base_task<br/>(task/base_task.py)"]
    end

    G --> A1
    API --> A1
    GS --> A1
    A1 --> TR
    A1 --> Ret
    A1 --> DL
    A1 --> KH
    TR --> Ret
    A1 --> PY
    A1 --> R
    A1 --> BASH
    A1 --> MCP
    BE1 --> BT
```

At the top, users interact through either a **Gradio web demo** or the **Python API**. Both paths converge on the `A1` agent — the system's primary orchestration class. The A1 agent sits between the user and every resource in the system: it retrieves relevant tools, assembles data and software context, generates a system prompt, and drives the execution loop. Below the agent, the resource management layer provides the *what* (tools, data, knowledge), and the execution engine provides the *how* (Python, R, Bash, MCP). The evaluation layer sits to the side, offering a benchmark harness for measuring agent performance.

Sources: [a1.py](biomni/agent/a1.py#L56-L68), [react.py](biomni/agent/react.py#L38-L46)

## Package Structure

The `biomni/` package is organized into six functional directories, each encapsulating a distinct architectural concern. Understanding this layout is the key to navigating the codebase efficiently.

```
biomni/
├── agent/          # Agent classes (A1, ReAct, FunctionGenerator)
├── tool/           # 20+ domain tool modules, schemas, registry
├── model/          # Retrieval-Augmented tool selection
├── task/           # Benchmark task definitions & evaluation
├── know_how/       # Best-practice documents & protocols
├── eval/           # Evaluation harness (BiomniEval1)
├── config.py       # Centralized configuration
├── llm.py          # Multi-provider LLM factory
├── env_desc.py     # Data lake & software library descriptors
├── env_desc_cm.py  # Commercial-mode filtered descriptors
└── utils.py        # Shared utilities (REPL, parsers, helpers)
```

The **`agent/`** directory contains the orchestrators — classes that combine an LLM with tools and data into a loop. The **`tool/`** directory is the largest, housing domain-specific function modules (genomics, pharmacology, imaging, etc.), pre-computed API schemas for 30+ external databases, and the tool registry. The **`model/`** directory provides retrieval logic that prunes the full resource catalog down to a query-relevant subset. The **`task/`** and **`eval/`** directories handle benchmarking. The **`know_how/`** directory stores curated markdown documents with expert protocols and best practices.

Sources: [a1.py](biomni/agent/a1.py#L225-L232), [tool_registry.py](biomni/tool/tool_registry.py#L6-L18), [retriever.py](biomni/model/retriever.py#L8-L14)

## The A1 Agent: Core Orchestration

The `A1` class in [biomni/agent/a1.py](biomni/agent/a1.py) is the central orchestrator — a 3000-line class that manages the entire lifecycle of a biomedical problem-solving session. It implements a **state-machine workflow** built on LangGraph, where each turn the agent either generates a plan, executes code, or delivers a final solution.

### Agent State Model

The agent tracks its progress through an `AgentState` TypedDict containing two fields: a `messages` list accumulating the full conversation, and a `next_step` string that routes control flow.

| Field | Type | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `messages` | `list[BaseMessage]` | Accumulated conversation history (Human, AI, System, Tool messages) |
| `next_step` | `str \| None` | Routing directive: `"generate"`, `"execute"`, or `"end"` |

This state drives a three-node graph inside the `configure()` method: **generate** → **execute** → **generate** (looping) or **end**. The `generate` node invokes the LLM with the system prompt and conversation history, then parses the response for XML tags to determine the next routing. The `execute` node runs the extracted code (Python, R, or Bash) and feeds observations back into the message list.

Sources: [a1.py](biomni/agent/a1.py#L51-L55), [a1.py](biomni/agent/a1.py#L1289-L1369)

### Initialization Pipeline

When you instantiate `A1(path, llm, ...)`, the constructor orchestrates a multi-step initialization pipeline:

1. **Configuration resolution** — Parameters fall back to `BiomniConfig` defaults, which themselves fall back to environment variables like `BIOMNI_LLM`, `BIOMNI_PATH`, and `BIOMNI_COMMERCIAL_MODE`.
2. **Mode selection** — If `commercial_mode=True`, the agent imports from `env_desc_cm` (filtered descriptors) instead of `env_desc`, excluding non-commercial datasets and know-how documents.
3. **Data lake bootstrapping** — Creates `biomni_data/data_lake/` and `biomni_data/benchmark/` directories, then downloads missing files from `https://biomni-release.s3.amazonaws.com`.
4. **LLM instantiation** — Calls `get_llm()` which supports seven providers: OpenAI, AzureOpenAI, Anthropic, Ollama, Gemini, Bedrock, Groq, and a Custom mode for self-hosted endpoints.
5. **Tool loading** — Calls `read_module2api()` which scans all domain modules under `biomni/tool/`, parsing `@tool`-decorated functions into a `module2api` dictionary mapping module names to API schema lists.
6. **Registry creation** — If `use_tool_retriever=True`, a `ToolRegistry` is built from the full module2api dictionary, and a `ToolRetriever` is attached.
7. **Know-how loading** — A `KnowHowLoader` discovers and parses all markdown documents from `biomni/know_how/resource/`, extracting metadata headers and stripping them for agent context.
8. **Initial configuration** — Calls `self.configure()` to build the system prompt and LangGraph workflow.

Sources: [a1.py](biomni/agent/a1.py#L56-L225), [config.py](biomni/config.py#L12-L99), [llm.py](biomni/llm.py#L9-L22)

### The Execution Loop

The `go(prompt)` method triggers the main execution loop, which follows this sequence:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    P["User Prompt"] --> RQ{"Tool Retriever<br/>Enabled?"}
    RQ -- Yes --> RET["Retrieve relevant<br/>tools, data, libraries,<br/>know-how via LLM"]
    RQ -- No --> INIT["Use full resource<br/>catalog in system prompt"]
    RET --> UPD["Update system prompt<br/>with selected resources"]
    INIT --> LG
    UPD --> LG["LangGraph Stream<br/>(recursion_limit=500)"]
    LG --> GEN["generate node:<br/>LLM produces response<br/>with plan + tags"]
    GEN --> PARSE{"Parse response tags"}
    PARSE -- "&lt;execute&gt; found" --> EXEC["execute node:<br/>Run code via REPL<br/>(Python/R/Bash)"]
    PARSE -- "&lt;solution&gt; found" --> END["end: Return<br/>final answer"]
    PARSE -- "No tags" --> ERR["Inject correction<br/>message, re-generate"]
    ERR --> GEN
    EXEC --> OBS["Append observation<br/>to messages"]
    OBS --> GEN
```

Each `generate` step sends the full message list (system prompt + conversation) to the LLM. The system prompt instructs the model to think with a reasoning block, then either wrap code in `<execute>` tags or wrap the final answer in `<solution>` tags. The parser uses regex matching with fallback patterns for different LLM formatting styles — including recovery for incomplete XML tags and markdown code blocks from OpenAI models. Code execution routes through a **persistent Python REPL** (shared global namespace across turns), an R subprocess runner, or a Bash subprocess, with configurable timeouts.

> [!TIP]
> The agent's persistent REPL means variables defined in one execution step survive into the next. This is intentional — it allows multi-step workflows like loading a dataset, transforming it, and then visualizing it across separate code blocks. The namespace is per-agent-instance, not per-invocation, so state persists across multiple `go()` calls within the same `A1` object.

Sources: [a1.py](biomni/agent/a1.py#L1381-L1488), [a1.py](biomni/agent/a1.py#L1759-L1789), [support_tools.py](biomni/tool/support_tools.py#L13-L16)

## Resource Management Layer

The resource management layer answers a fundamental question for each user query: *which tools, data, software, and knowledge should the agent know about?* This layer is split into two complementary systems — a full catalog used during initial configuration, and a retrieval-based subset selection used at query time.

### Data Lake

The data lake is a collection of **79 pre-indexed biomedical datasets** stored locally in `biomni_data/data_lake/`. These span protein interactions (BioPlex, STRING), cancer genomics (DepMap CRISPR screens, cell line omics), drug data (BindingDB, Broad Repurposing Hub), gene expression (GTEx, CZI Cell Census), variant databases (GeneBASS, GWAS Catalog), pathway and ontology data (MSigDB gene sets, Gene Ontology), and more. Each dataset is described in the `data_lake_dict` dictionary with a human-readable description that helps the agent understand what each file contains.

Sources: [env_desc.py](biomni/env_desc.py#L1-L79)

### Software Library

The `library_content_dict` describes **100+ available software packages** organized by type: Python packages (scanpy, rdkit, pysam, etc.), R packages (DESeq2, clusterProfiler, Seurat), and CLI tools (samtools, bowtie2, bedtools, macs2). Each entry includes its invocation pattern — for example, R packages note the `subprocess.run(['Rscript', '-e', ...])` pattern. These are *available* software, not imported by default; the agent writes import statements or subprocess calls as needed in its generated code.

Sources: [env_desc.py](biomni/env_desc.py#L82-L222)

### Tool System

The tool system is the largest subsystem, organized into **20+ domain-specific modules** that map biological disciplines to callable Python functions:

| Domain Module | Example Functions | Data Sources |
|---|---|---|
| `genomics.py` | Variant queries, gene set enrichment, genome coordinate conversion | Ensembl, NCBI, GWAS Catalog |
| `pharmacology.py` | Drug-target interaction, binding affinity lookup, drug repurposing | ChEMBL, DrugBank, BindingDB |
| `cell_biology.py` | scRNA-seq analysis, cell type annotation, trajectory inference | CZI Census, Scanpy |
| `genetics.py` | Gene ID conversion, genetic interaction lookup, CRISPR screen analysis | Entrez, Ensembl, DepMap |
| `database.py` | Cross-database queries (UniProt, KEGG, Reactome, PDB, etc.) | 30+ pre-built schemas |
| `protocols.py` | Protocol search (Protocols.io), local protocol management | Protocols.io API |
| `support_tools.py` | Python REPL execution, matplotlib plot capture | Local environment |

Each domain module exports `@tool`-decorated functions with complete docstrings and type annotations. The `read_module2api()` utility scans these modules at import time and builds the `module2api` dictionary — a nested mapping of `{module_name: [{name, description, required_parameters, ...}, ...]}` that the agent uses to understand its available functions. The `schema_db/` directory contains 30+ pre-computed API schema pickles for major biomedical databases, avoiding the need for live schema discovery.

Sources: [utils.py](biomni/utils.py#L845-L879), [tool_registry.py](biomni/tool/tool_registry.py#L6-L18), [support_tools.py](biomni/tool/support_tools.py#L13-L16)

### Retrieval-Augmented Resource Selection

When `use_tool_retriever=True` (the default), the `ToolRetriever` in [biomni/model/retriever.py](biomni/model/retriever.py) performs a **prompt-based retrieval** step before each query. Rather than using vector embeddings, it constructs a detailed prompt listing all available tools (with descriptions and parameters), data lake items, software libraries, and know-how documents, then asks the agent's own LLM to select the relevant subset. This produces four filtered lists — tools, data, libraries, and know-how — that replace the full catalog in the system prompt.

The retrieval prompt explicitly instructs the LLM to be "generous in selection" to avoid missing potentially useful resources. The `ToolRetriever` class also handles response parsing for both plain-text and Responses API-style content blocks, making it compatible with multiple LLM providers.

Sources: [retriever.py](biomni/model/retriever.py#L14-L50), [a1.py](biomni/agent/a1.py#L1646-L1757)

### Know-How Library

The `KnowHowLoader` in [biomni/know_how/loader.py](biomni/know_how/loader.py) manages a collection of **curated markdown documents** containing expert protocols, best practices, and troubleshooting guides (e.g., sgRNA design guides, single-cell annotation workflows). Each document has a YAML-like metadata header (name, description, commercial_use license) followed by free-form content. During configuration, all know-how documents are loaded into the initial system prompt so best practices are always available. During retrieval, only query-relevant documents are surfaced with their full content injected into the system prompt.

> [!TIP]
> Know-how documents are always included in the initial system prompt regardless of the retrieval setting. This design ensures that foundational best practices (like experimental design principles) are never missed, while retrieval adds domain-specific depth on top.

Sources: [loader.py](biomni/know_how/loader.py#L8-L30), [a1.py](biomni/agent/a1.py#L1351-L1366)

## Multi-Provider LLM Abstraction

The LLM layer in [biomni/llm.py](biomni/llm.py) provides a unified factory function `get_llm()` that abstracts across seven backend providers. The `SourceType` literal enforces allowed values at the type level, and the factory returns a LangChain `BaseChatModel` instance regardless of provider. This means the entire agent — including the retriever's LLM calls — works identically whether you're using Anthropic Claude, OpenAI GPT, a local Ollama model, or a custom endpoint via `base_url` and `api_key`.

| Provider | Source Type | Key Requirement |
|---|---|---|
| Anthropic Claude | `"Anthropic"` | `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` env var |
| OpenAI GPT | `"OpenAI"` | `OPENAI_API_KEY` env var |
| Azure OpenAI | `"AzureOpenAI"` | `AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY` + endpoint |
| Google Gemini | `"Gemini"` | `GOOGLE_API_KEY` env var |
| AWS Bedrock | `"Bedrock"` | AWS credentials configured |
| Groq | `"Groq"` | `GROQ_API_KEY` env var |
| Ollama (local) | `"Ollama"` | Local Ollama server running |
| Custom endpoint | `"Custom"` | `base_url` + `api_key` params |

The default model is `claude-sonnet-4-5`, configurable via `BiomniConfig.llm` or the `BIOMNI_LLM` environment variable. Stop sequences are set to `["</execute>", "</solution>"]` to help the LLM delimit its output correctly.

Sources: [llm.py](biomni/llm.py#L9-L22), [config.py](biomni/config.py#L36-L37)

## Configuration System

The `BiomniConfig` dataclass in [biomni/config.py](biomni/config.py) centralizes all configurable parameters with sensible defaults and a two-tier override mechanism: constructor arguments → environment variables. A global `default_config` singleton is created at module load time, and the `A1.__init__()` constructor resolves each parameter against this singleton.

| Parameter | Default | Environment Variable | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `path` | `"./data"` | `BIOMNI_PATH` / `BIOMNI_DATA_PATH` | Root data directory |
| `llm` | `"claude-sonnet-4-5"` | `BIOMNI_LLM` / `BIOMNI_LLM_MODEL` | LLM model identifier |
| `temperature` | `0.7` | `BIOMNI_TEMPERATURE` | LLM sampling temperature |
| `timeout_seconds` | `600` | `BIOMNI_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` | Code execution timeout |
| `use_tool_retriever` | `True` | `BIOMNI_USE_TOOL_RETRIEVER` | Enable retrieval-augmented selection |
| `commercial_mode` | `False` | `BIOMNI_COMMERCIAL_MODE` | Exclude non-commercial datasets |
| `source` | `None` (auto-detect) | `BIOMNI_SOURCE` | LLM provider |
| `base_url` | `None` | `BIOMNI_CUSTOM_BASE_URL` | Custom model endpoint |
| `api_key` | `None` | `BIOMNI_CUSTOM_API_KEY` | Custom model API key |

The `commercial_mode` flag triggers a cascade: it switches the data lake and software descriptors to filtered versions (`env_desc_cm` instead of `env_desc`), and removes know-how documents whose metadata marks them as non-commercial. This is the architectural mechanism that enforces licensing compliance.

Sources: [config.py](biomni/config.py#L12-L99), [a1.py](biomni/agent/a1.py#L57-L82)

## Evaluation Architecture

The evaluation subsystem sits alongside the agent and provides a standardized harness for benchmarking. The `BiomniEval1` class in [biomni/eval/biomni_eval1.py](biomni/eval/biomni_eval1.py) loads a merged Parquet dataset containing all BiomniEval1 task instances, then provides `evaluate(task_name, instance_id, user_answer)` with task-specific reward computation logic. The `base_task` class in [biomni/task/base_task.py](biomni/task/base_task.py) defines a minimal interface for evaluation tasks: `get_example()`, `get_iterator()`, `evaluate()`, `output_class()`, and `get_prompt_from_input()`.

Sources: [biomni_eval1.py](biomni/eval/biomni_eval1.py#L14-L30), [base_task.py](biomni/task/base_task.py#L1-L19)

## Agent Variants

Beyond the primary `A1` agent, the framework provides three auxiliary agent classes, each serving a distinct purpose in the broader workflow:

| Agent | Location | Purpose | Key Difference from A1 |
|---|---|---|---|
| `A1` | `agent/a1.py` | Primary biomedical problem-solver | Full resource management, persistent REPL, XML-tag protocol |
| `react` | `agent/react.py` | LangGraph ReAct agent | Uses standard LangGraph tool-calling, supports plan/reflect modes |
| `FunctionGenerator` | `agent/function_generator.py` | Standalone code generator | Generates executable Python scripts from task descriptions |
| `PaperTaskExtractor` | `agent/env_collection.py` | Academic paper analyzer | Extracts generalizable tasks from papers via chunked processing |
| `qa_llm` | `agent/qa_llm.py` | Simple QA baseline | Direct LLM question-answering without tools |

The `react` class offers an alternative execution paradigm — it uses LangGraph's built-in tool-calling mechanism rather than the XML-tag protocol that A1 uses, and supports explicit planning (`plan=True`) and reflection (`reflect=True`) modes. The `FunctionGenerator` and `PaperTaskExtractor` are specialized utility agents used in benchmark construction rather than end-user interaction.

Sources: [react.py](biomni/agent/react.py#L38-L46), [function_generator.py](biomni/agent/function_generator.py#L22-L25), [env_collection.py](biomni/agent/env_collection.py#L12-L15)

## Extensibility Points

The architecture exposes four primary extension mechanisms that allow you to customize the agent without modifying core internals:

1. **Custom Tools** — `agent.add_tool(api)` registers a new callable function into the tool registry, making it available for retrieval and import in generated code. The agent also tracks custom tools separately and highlights them in the system prompt with a 🔧 prefix.

2. **Custom Data** — `agent.add_data(data)` adds files to the data lake with descriptions, updating both the internal data lake and the descriptor dictionary. Custom data is highlighted with a 📊 prefix.

3. **Custom Software** — `agent.add_software(software)` extends the available library catalog, highlighted with a ⚙️ prefix.

4. **MCP Integration** — `agent.add_mcp(config_path)` connects to external Model Context Protocol servers, importing their tools into the agent's tool registry. `agent.create_mcp_server()` can also expose the agent's own tools as an MCP server for other clients.

Each extension mechanism triggers an automatic `configure()` call to rebuild the system prompt with the updated resource set.

Sources: [a1.py](biomni/agent/a1.py#L225-L232), [a1.py](biomni/agent/a1.py#L676-L685), [a1.py](biomni/agent/a1.py#L777-L786), [a1.py](biomni/agent/a1.py#L350-L360)
