## Database Query Integration Layer

The `database.py` module is the system's largest and most interconnected domain module, providing a unified gateway to over 30 external bioinformatics databases and APIs. Each query function follows a consistent two-tier dispatch pattern: the agent provides a natural-language `prompt` (and optionally a specific `endpoint`), and the function resolves the appropriate API call through a schema-driven LLM routing step or a direct endpoint lookup. The schema databases stored as pickle files in [`tool/schema_db/`](biomni/tool/schema_db/) (e.g., `uniprot.pkl`, `kegg.pkl`, `pubchem.pkl`, `chembl.pkl`) pre-define the available endpoints and parameter structures for each external service.
Sources: [database.py](biomni/tool/database.py#L111-L205), [database.py](biomni/tool/database.py#L448-L544)

The query functions fall into four architectural categories based on how they resolve the agent's intent:

**Schema-routed queries** accept a natural-language `prompt` and use an LLM to select the correct API endpoint from the pre-serialized schema. Functions like [`query_uniprot()`](biomni/tool/database.py#L448-L544), [`query_kegg()`](biomni/tool/database.py#L1030-L1119), and [`query_stringdb()`](biomni/tool/database.py#L1119-L1286) follow this pattern. The `_query_llm_for_api()` helper sends the schema, available endpoints, and the user prompt to a small language model, which returns a structured endpoint-and-parameters dict.

**Direct-endpoint queries** allow the agent to specify an explicit API endpoint URL, bypassing LLM routing. This is used when the ReAct agent has already identified the exact resource. Functions like [`query_alphafold()`](biomni/tool/database.py#L544-L693), [`query_pdb()`](biomni/tool/database.py#L800-L917), and [`query_pdb_identifiers()`](biomni/tool/database.py#L917-L1030) accept an `endpoint` parameter for targeted retrieval.

**NCBI Entrez queries** leverage Biopython's Entrez module for standardized access to NCBI databases. The internal [`_query_ncbi_database()`](biomni/tool/database.py#L199-L317) handles E-utilities calls with built-in rate limiting and result formatting.

**GraphQL queries** target APIs like Open Targets, which expose a GraphQL interface. The [`execute_graphql_query()`](biomni/utils.py#L341-L346) utility in `utils.py` provides the transport layer, and [`query_opentarget()`](biomni/tool/database.py#L2315-L2415) wraps it with prompt-driven parameter extraction.

> [!TIP]
> The `prompt` parameter in database query tools is not merely documentation — it is the primary dispatch mechanism. When the ReAct agent calls `query_uniprot(prompt="Find kinase domains in human proteins")`, this string is routed to a small LLM that maps it against the UniProt API schema to select the correct endpoint and parameters. Omitting `prompt` and providing only `endpoint` skips this routing step entirely, yielding faster but more brittle invocations.

## Molecular Biology Workbench

The [`molecular_biology.py`](biomni/tool/molecular_biology.py) module implements a complete in-silico cloning and sequence engineering pipeline. Its tools form a coherent workflow chain: from plasmid annotation through restriction analysis, PCR simulation, primer design, and multi-fragment assembly. This is one of the most deeply integrated modules, where tool outputs naturally feed into downstream tool inputs.
Sources: [molecular_biology.py](biomni/tool/molecular_biology.py#L167-L958)

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph "Sequence Input"
        AP[annotate_plasmid<br/>or annotate_open_reading_frames]
        GS[get_plasmid_sequence<br/>or get_gene_coding_sequence]
    end

    subgraph "Restriction Analysis"
        FR[find_restriction_enzymes]
        DS[digest_sequence]
        FS[find_restriction_sites]
    end

    subgraph "Amplification & Assembly"
        DP[design_primer]
        PCR[pcr_simple]
        GGA[golden_gate_assembly]
        DGO[design_golden_gate_oligos]
    end

    subgraph "Verification"
        DVP[design_verification_primers]
        SM[find_sequence_mutations]
    end

    AP & GS --> FR
    FR --> DS
    FR --> FS
    DS --> DP
    DP --> PCR
    DP --> GGA
    AP --> DGO
    DGO --> GGA
    PCR --> DVP
    GGA --> DVP
    PCR --> SM
```

Key implementation details: [`annotate_plasmid()`](biomni/tool/molecular_biology.py#L167-L252) performs *de novo* ORF detection and feature annotation on arbitrary sequences, supporting both linear and circular topologies. [`digest_sequence()`](biomni/tool/molecular_biology.py#L602-L725) uses BioPython's restriction enzyme library to perform in-silico digests, returning fragment sizes and cut positions. The [`golden_gate_assembly()`](biomni/tool/molecular_biology.py#L1849-L2223) function simulates Type IIS restriction-ligation assembly, checking for compatible overhangs and predicting assembly outcomes.
Sources: [molecular_biology.py](biomni/tool/molecular_biology.py#L167-L252), [molecular_biology.py](biomni/tool/molecular_biology.py#L602-L725), [molecular_biology.py](biomni/tool/molecular_biology.py#L1849-L2223)

## Pharmacology and Drug Safety

The [`pharmacology.py`](biomni/tool/pharmacology.py) module is the second-largest implementation and covers the drug discovery-to-safety continuum. It spans molecular docking, ADMET prediction, drug-drug interaction querying, and FDA regulatory surveillance. Notably, this module contains the [`OpenFDAClient`](biomni/tool/pharmacology.py#L3457-L3641) class — one of the few OOP patterns in the tool layer — which wraps the OpenFDA REST API with retry logic, rate limiting, and structured response parsing.
Sources: [pharmacology.py](biomni/tool/pharmacology.py#L13-L14), [pharmacology.py](biomni/tool/pharmacology.py#L3457-L3641)

| Sub-domain | Tools | Data Sources |
|---|---|---|
| Molecular Docking | `run_diffdock_with_smiles`, `docking_autodock_vina`, `run_autosite` | PDB structures, SMILES inputs |
| ADMET & Binding | `predict_admet_properties`, `predict_binding_affinity_protein_1d_sequence`, `calculate_physicochemical_properties` | Graph neural networks, MPNN models |
| Drug Repurposing | `retrieve_topk_repurposing_drugs_from_disease_txgnn` | TxGNN pretrained model + data lake |
| Drug Interactions | `query_drug_interactions`, `check_drug_combination_safety`, `analyze_interaction_mechanisms`, `find_alternative_drugs_ddinter` | DDInter database (data lake) |
| FDA Surveillance | `query_fda_adverse_events`, `get_fda_drug_label_info`, `check_fda_drug_recalls`, `analyze_fda_safety_signals` | OpenFDA API |
| Preclinical | `analyze_xenograft_tumor_growth_inhibition`, `analyze_accelerated_stability_of_pharmaceutical_formulations`, `grade_adverse_events_using_vcog_ctcae` | CSV/Excel data files |
| Imaging Analysis | `analyze_western_blot`, `analyze_pixel_distribution`, `find_roi_from_image` | Blot images, microscopy |

The drug interaction subsystem is particularly sophisticated. [`query_drug_interactions()`](biomni/tool/pharmacology.py#L2801-L2932) loads the DDInter dataset from the data lake, builds an interaction matrix with standardized drug name mapping, and supports filtering by interaction type and severity. [`check_drug_combination_safety()`](biomni/tool/pharmacology.py#L2932-L3097) extends this to accept an arbitrary drug list and returns a comprehensive safety assessment including mechanism-of-action analysis and clinical management recommendations.
Sources: [pharmacology.py](biomni/tool/pharmacology.py#L2460-L2694), [pharmacology.py](biomni/tool/pharmacology.py#L2801-L2932)

> [!TIP]
> Several pharmacology tools depend on data lake files (e.g., DDInter interaction data, TxGNN model checkpoints) that are not bundled with the repository. The `data_lake_path` parameter is required for `query_drug_interactions`, `check_drug_combination_safety`, and `retrieve_topk_repurposing_drugs_from_disease_txgnn`. If these files are absent, the tools fall back to returning guidance messages rather than raising hard errors. See [Data Lake Management](16-data-lake-management) for setup instructions.

## Single-Cell and Omics Analysis (Genomics)

The [`genomics.py`](biomni/tool/genomics.py) module addresses the single-cell transcriptomics and epigenomics workflow. It provides end-to-end capabilities from raw data processing through embedding generation, cell type annotation, and gene set enrichment. The module is notable for integrating multiple embedding strategies (scVI, Harmony, UCE, STATE, TranscriptFormer) and offering both automated LLM-based and reference-mapping approaches to cell type annotation.
Sources: [genomics.py](biomni/tool/genomics.py#L463-L870)

The [`unsupervised_celltype_transfer_between_scRNA_datasets()`](biomni/tool/genomics.py#L18-L107) function serves as a meta-orchestrator: it accepts an annotated reference and an unannotated query dataset, then runs one or more of ten transfer methods (SCANVI_POPV, KNN-BBKNN, KNN-Harmony, ONCLASS, etc.) selected via boolean flags. This multi-method approach lets the agent compare annotation strategies. The [`annotate_celltype_scRNA()`](biomni/tool/genomics.py#L463-L600) function takes a different approach — it performs Leiden clustering, extracts differentially expressed genes, and sends them to a large language model for semantic cell type naming, bridging computational analysis with domain knowledge.
Sources: [genomics.py](biomni/tool/genomics.py#L18-L107), [genomics.py](biomni/tool/genomics.py#L463-L600)

For epigenomics, [`perform_chipseq_peak_calling_with_macs2()`](biomni/tool/genomics.py#L1617-L1794) wraps the MACS2 peak caller, while [`find_enriched_motifs_with_homer()`](biomni/tool/genomics.py#L1794-L1965) chains peak calling into motif discovery. The [`analyze_chromatin_interactions()`](biomni/tool/genomics.py#L1091-L1424) and [`analyze_genomic_region_overlap()`](biomni/tool/genomics.py#L1965-L2167) functions handle Hi-C data and comparative genomics respectively, completing the epigenomic analysis pipeline.
Sources: [genomics.py](biomni/tool/genomics.py#L1617-L1965), [genomics.py](biomni/tool/genomics.py#L1091-L1424)

## Bioimaging: OOP Within the Flat-Function Paradigm

The [`bioimaging.py`](biomni/tool/bioimaging.py) module is architecturally distinct: it defines two stateful tool classes — [`SegmentationTool`](biomni/tool/bioimaging.py#L30-L579) and [`ImageRegistrationTool`](biomni/tool/bioimaging.py#L579-L868) — but exposes them through stateless convenience functions that the registry can index. This hybrid pattern allows internal complexity (model downloading, environment setup, multi-step pipelines) while maintaining the flat-function contract at the agent boundary.
Sources: [bioimaging.py](biomni/tool/bioimaging.py#L30-L579), [bioimaging.py](biomni/tool/bioimaging.py#L959-L1009)

The segmentation pipeline leverages nnUNet for medical image segmentation with automatic model downloading from Zenodo. [`segment_with_nn_unet()`](biomni/tool/bioimaging.py#L977-L1006) handles the full workflow: modality splitting for BRATS-style multi-channel inputs, environment variable configuration, model inference with optional test-time augmentation, and visualization generation. The registration pipeline uses SimpleITK and provides three transform levels — [`quick_rigid_registration()`](biomni/tool/bioimaging.py#L1034-L1109), [`quick_affine_registration()`](biomni/tool/bioimaging.py#L1110-L1185), and [`quick_deformable_registration()`](biomni/tool/bioimaging.py#L1186-L1263) — each with preprocessing, multi-metric optimization, and similarity scoring.
Sources: [bioimaging.py](biomni/tool/bioimaging.py#L977-L1006), [bioimaging.py](biomni/tool/bioimaging.py#L1034-L1263)

## Literature and Knowledge Retrieval

The [`literature.py`](biomni/tool/literature.py) module provides the agent's window into external scientific knowledge. It implements both direct database queries (PubMed, arXiv, Google Scholar) and broader web search capabilities through Claude-powered search with content extraction. [`query_pubmed()`](biomni/tool/literature.py#L144-L185) uses Biopython's Entrez interface with configurable result limits and retry logic, while [`advanced_web_search_claude()`](biomni/tool/literature.py#L218-L303) chains web search with URL content extraction for accessing paywalled or supplementary materials. The [`fetch_supplementary_info_from_doi()`](biomni/tool/literature.py#L13-L89) function resolves DOIs to supplementary data downloads.
Sources: [literature.py](biomni/tool/literature.py#L13-L303)

## Protocol Retrieval System

The [`protocols.py`](biomni/tool/protocols.py) module operates alongside a curated local protocol library stored in [`tool/protocols/`](biomni/tool/protocols/) containing approximately 100+ text files from two major sources: **Addgene** (47 protocols covering molecular cloning, virus production, and general lab techniques) and **Thermo Fisher Scientific** (38 protocols covering flow cytometry, cell culture, staining, and viability assays). The module provides three operations: [`search_protocols()`](biomni/tool/protocols.py#L29-L133) queries the protocols.io API, [`list_local_protocols()`](biomni/tool/protocols.py#L180-L242) enumerates the local text library with optional source filtering, and [`read_local_protocol()`](biomni/tool/protocols.py#L243-L306) retrieves the full text of a specific protocol. This dual local/remote architecture ensures the agent can access standardized lab procedures even without internet connectivity.
Sources: [protocols.py](biomni/tool/protocols.py#L29-L306), [protocols/](biomni/tool/protocols/)

## Support and Execution Infrastructure

Beyond domain-specific tools, the [`support_tools.py`](biomni/tool/support_tools.py) module provides the runtime execution substrate. Its centerpiece is [`run_python_repl()`](biomni/tool/support_tools.py#L13-L46), a persistent Python REPL that maintains variable state across invocations — this is how the agent chains multi-step analyses where intermediate results must persist. The module also includes automatic matplotlib plot capture through monkey-patching ([`_apply_matplotlib_patches()`](biomni/tool/support_tools.py#L81-L128)), enabling the agent to generate and return visualizations without explicit file I/O. The [`read_function_source_code()`](biomni/tool/support_tools.py#L141-L198) function lets the agent introspect tool implementations at runtime, supporting self-documenting behavior during complex reasoning chains.
Sources: [support_tools.py](biomni/tool/support_tools.py#L13-L198)

## Execution Model and Timeout Safety

All tool functions execute within a timeout wrapper defined by [`run_with_timeout()`](biomni/utils.py#L183-L244), which defaults to 600 seconds per invocation. This threading-based timeout (rather than multiprocessing) is a deliberate choice: it preserves the global variable namespace across calls, which is essential for the persistent REPL pattern. When a timeout occurs, the function returns an error string rather than raising an exception, allowing the agent's ReAct loop to gracefully recover and attempt alternative approaches.
Sources: [utils.py](biomni/utils.py#L183-L244)

## Cross-References

- The mechanism by which the agent selects among these tools at runtime is covered in [Retrieval-Augmented Tool Selection](13-retrieval-augmented-tool-selection).
- How tools are registered, validated, and indexed is detailed in [Tool Registry and Discovery](12-tool-registry-and-discovery).
- For extending the system with new domain tools, see [Custom Tools and Data](18-custom-tools-and-data).
- Database schema files and their role in query routing are described in [Database Query Integrations](15-database-query-integrations).
- Environment dependencies required by these tools are documented in [Environment Setup and Dependencies](22-environment-setup-and-dependencies).

# Database Query Integrations



Biomni abstracts over **35+ external biological databases** through a unified natural-language query interface, converting free-form scientific questions into structured API calls. This layer is the primary bridge between the agent's reasoning engine and the vast landscape of publicly available bioinformatics resources — from protein structure databases like AlphaFold and PDB, through genomic variant repositories like ClinVar and gnomAD, to drug databases like ChEMBL and OpenFDA. The entire system is defined in a single, ~5000-line module that follows a remarkably consistent architectural pattern across all integrations.

## Architectural Overview

The database integration layer sits between the agent's tool-selection mechanism and the external API surface. Every query function follows a dual-mode design: it accepts either a **natural language prompt** (which an LLM translates into a structured API call) or a **direct endpoint/parameter** (which bypasses LLM mediation entirely). This duality enables both autonomous agent operation and programmatic direct usage.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Agent["Agent Layer"]
        A1["A1 Agent"] -->|selects tool| TR["Tool Retriever"]
        TR -->|matches description| TD["Tool Description Registry"]
    end

    subgraph DBLayer["Database Query Layer<br/>biomni/tool/database.py"]
        direction TB
        QF["query_uniprot, query_pdb, ...<br/>35+ query functions"]
        QF -->|"prompt mode"| LLM["_query_llm_for_api()"]
        QF -->|"direct mode"| REST["_query_rest_api()"]
        QF -->|"NCBI family"| NCBI["_query_ncbi_database()"]
        QF -->|"sequence search"| BLAST["blast_sequence()"]
        LLM -->|generates URL/query| REST
        NCBI -->|"ESearch + ESummary"| REST
    end

    subgraph Schema["Schema Cache"]
        SP["uniprot.pkl, pdb.pkl, ...<br/>32 serialized schemas"]
    end

    subgraph External["External APIs"]
        E1["UniProt REST"]
        E2["RCSB PDB"]
        E3["NCBI E-utilities"]
        E4["KEGG"]
        E5["AlphaFold"]
        E6["OpenTargets GraphQL"]
        E7["gnomAD GraphQL"]
        E8["...30+ more"]
    end

    TD --> QF
    LLM -.->|loads schema| SP
    REST --> E1
    REST --> E2
    REST --> E4
    REST --> E5
    REST --> E6
    REST --> E7
    REST --> E8
    NCBI --> E3
```

The key insight is that **every query function is both a tool for the agent and a standalone API**. The agent discovers them through the tool description registry, but developers can call them directly with either natural language or structured parameters.

Sources: [database.py](biomni/tool/database.py#L1-L16), [database.py](biomni/tool/database.py#L448-L468)

## The Three Integration Patterns

All 35+ database integrations fall into one of three architectural patterns, distinguished by how the natural-language prompt is translated into an API request and what protocol the target database speaks.

### Pattern 1: LLM-Mediated REST API Translation

This is the most common pattern, used by databases that expose REST APIs with complex URL structures and query syntax. The flow is: **prompt → LLM (with schema) → URL construction → REST call**. The LLM receives a serialized API schema from a `.pkl` file and a domain-specific system prompt that encodes the API's conventions. It returns a JSON object containing the complete URL and a description of what the query does.

UniProt exemplifies this pattern perfectly. When a user asks "Find information about human insulin," the function loads `schema_db/uniprot.pkl`, constructs a system prompt that teaches the LLM about UniProt's accession formats, organism taxonomy IDs, and query fields, then sends the natural language to the configured LLM. The LLM returns something like `{"full_url": "https://rest.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/search?query=insulin+AND+organism_id:9606", "description": "..."}`, and the function passes that URL directly to `_query_rest_api()`.

Sources: [database.py](biomni/tool/database.py#L448-L543), [database.py](biomni/tool/database.py#L693-L800)

### Pattern 2: LLM-Mediated Query Generation for Structured APIs

Some databases — particularly GraphQL endpoints and NCBI E-utilities — don't accept URLs with query parameters but instead expect structured JSON or specialized query syntax. Here, the LLM generates a **query object** (a JSON search request for PDB, a GraphQL string for OpenTargets, or a search term string for ClinVar) rather than a URL.

For example, `query_pdb()` asks the LLM to generate a structured RCSB Search API JSON document with terminal nodes, group operators, and return types. `query_clinvar()` asks the LLM to produce a ClinVar-syntax search string like `"BRCA1[gene] AND clinsig_pathogenic[prop]"` which is then passed to `_query_ncbi_database()`. `query_gnomad()` and `query_opentarget()` generate full GraphQL query strings with variable bindings.

Sources: [database.py](biomni/tool/database.py#L1824-L1906), [database.py](biomni/tool/database.py#L2315-L2400), [database.py](biomni/tool/database.py#L2753-L2850)

### Pattern 3: Direct Programmatic APIs

A small number of integrations bypass LLM mediation entirely because their APIs are simple enough (or unique enough) to warrant direct programmatic access. These include `query_alphafold()` (which constructs URLs from a UniProt ID, endpoint type, and model version), `blast_sequence()` (which uses BioPython's `NCBIWWW.qblast`), and the ENCODE Screen API functions `region_to_ccre_screen()` and `get_genes_near_ccre()` which accept genomic coordinates directly.

Sources: [database.py](biomni/tool/database.py#L544-L692), [database.py](biomni/tool/database.py#L2852-L2953), [database.py](biomni/tool/database.py#L3409-L3575)

## Infrastructure Layer: The Shared Query Engine

Four internal helper functions form the backbone of all database integrations. Understanding them is essential for anyone extending the system.

### `_query_rest_api()` — The Universal HTTP Client

This function is the lowest-level building block, handling GET and POST requests with uniform error handling, JSON parsing, and response wrapping. Every REST API integration eventually routes through this function. It returns a standardized dictionary with `success`, `query_info`, and `result` (or `error`) keys, ensuring that all 35+ query functions produce consistent output shapes for downstream consumers.

The error handling is particularly robust: it inspects HTTP error responses for known error key patterns (`messages`, `message`, `error`, `detail`) and extracts the most informative message rather than propagating raw HTTP status text.

Sources: [database.py](biomni/tool/database.py#L111-L198)

### `_query_llm_for_api()` — The NL-to-API Translator

This function takes a natural language prompt, a serialized schema dictionary, and a system prompt template (with a `{schema}` placeholder). It loads the LLM model from the global configuration (`default_config.llm`), formats the schema into the template, invokes the LLM, and then extracts a JSON object from the response by finding the first `{` and last `}` boundaries. This boundary-detection approach gracefully handles LLMs that prepend or append explanatory text around the JSON.

Sources: [database.py](biomni/tool/database.py#L36-L110)

### `_query_ncbi_database()` — The NCBI E-Utilities Pipeline

NCBI hosts multiple databases (ClinVar, GEO, dbSNP, PubChem) through a unified E-utilities interface. This helper implements the two-step NCBI workflow: first an ESearch request to get matching record IDs (using the history server for efficiency), then an ESummary request to fetch details for those IDs. Functions like `query_clinvar()`, `query_geo()`, and `query_dbsnp()` all delegate to this after the LLM generates the appropriate search term.

Sources: [database.py](biomni/tool/database.py#L199-L316)

### `_format_query_results()` — The Response Condenser

Many database APIs return verbose responses with nested structures that would overwhelm the agent's context window. This recursive formatter applies configurable rules: it truncates long strings, summarizes long lists (showing a sample with count metadata), limits recursion depth, and can include or exclude specific top-level keys. The default configuration caps list items at 5, string length at 100 characters, and excludes `raw_response`, `debug_info`, and `request_details` keys.

Sources: [database.py](biomni/tool/database.py#L317-L447)

> [!TIP]
> Every database query function returns a **consistent dictionary shape** — either `{"success": True, "query_info": {...}, "result": ...}` or `{"success": False, "error": "..."}`. When building custom tools or extending the system, always wrap your API calls through `_query_rest_api()` to maintain this contract. The agent's error recovery logic depends on this uniformity.

## Schema Cache: How the LLM Learns API Structure

The `schema_db/` directory contains 32 serialized Python pickle files — one for each LLM-mediated database integration. These schemas are loaded at query time by the respective query function and injected into the LLM's system prompt. Each schema captures the API's endpoint structure, available operations, required parameters, and domain-specific conventions.

The file naming convention is straightforward: the pickle file name matches the database name used in the function (e.g., `uniprot.pkl` for `query_uniprot`, `pdb.pkl` for `query_pdb`, `gnomad.pkl` for `query_gnomad`). The contents vary by API complexity — REST API schemas typically document URL patterns, query parameters, and response formats, while GraphQL schemas document types, queries, and mutations.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["query_uniprot(prompt='...')"] --> B["Load schema_db/uniprot.pkl"]
    B --> C["Inject into system_template"]
    C --> D["LLM generates full_url"]
    D --> E["_query_rest_api(url)"]
    E --> F["External UniProt API"]
```

> [!TIP]
> Schema files are binary pickles, not editable text. To update a database's schema, you must regenerate the `.pkl` file programmatically. When adding a new database integration, follow the convention: create a schema pickle in `schema_db/`, add the query function in `database.py`, and register its description in `tool_description/database.py`.

Sources: [schema_db/](biomni/tool/schema_db/), [database.py](biomni/tool/database.py#L480-L485)

## Tool Discovery: How the Agent Finds Database Tools

The agent doesn't call database functions directly by name. Instead, it uses the [Retrieval-Augmented Tool Selection](13-retrieval-augmented-tool-selection) system, which matches natural language queries against tool descriptions stored in `tool_description/database.py`. This file contains a structured list where each entry specifies the function name, a human-readable description, required parameters, and optional parameters with their types and defaults.

When the agent receives a task like "Find pathogenic BRCA1 variants," the retriever scores all tool descriptions against this query and selects the most relevant ones — in this case, `query_clinvar` and possibly `query_gnomad` or `query_cbioportal`. The agent then invokes the selected tool with an appropriate prompt, which triggers the LLM-mediated translation pipeline described above.

Sources: [tool_description/database.py](biomni/tool/tool_description/database.py#L1-L100), [retriever.py](biomni/model/retriever.py#L8-L16)

## Adding a New Database Integration

To integrate a new database, you need to create artifacts in three locations. The process follows a consistent pattern that mirrors the existing 35+ integrations.

**Step 1 — Create the schema file.** Generate a pickle file capturing the target API's endpoint structure, parameters, and conventions. Place it in `schema_db/<dbname>.pkl`.

**Step 2 — Implement the query function.** Add a `query_<dbname>()` function to `database.py`. Follow the established dual-mode pattern: accept both `prompt` (for LLM-mediated mode) and `endpoint`/`query`/`search_term` (for direct mode). Use `_query_llm_for_api()` with a domain-specific system template for NL translation, and `_query_rest_api()` for the actual HTTP call. Return the standardized dictionary format.

**Step 3 — Register the tool description.** Add an entry to the `description` list in `tool_description/database.py` with the function name, description text, required parameters, and optional parameters (including types and defaults).

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S1["1. Create schema_db/mydb.pkl"] --> S2["2. Add query_mydb() to database.py"]
    S2 --> S3["3. Register in tool_description/database.py"]
    S3 --> S4["4. Agent can discover and use the tool"]
```

For detailed guidance on the full tool registration lifecycle, including testing and validation, see [Custom Tools and Data](18-custom-tools-and-data). For understanding how the agent selects among all available tools at inference time, see [Retrieval-Augmented Tool Selection](13-retrieval-augmented-tool-selection).

Sources: [database.py](biomni/tool/database.py#L36-L110), [database.py](biomni/tool/database.py#L111-L198), [tool_description/database.py](biomni/tool/tool_description/database.py#L1-L100)

## Error Handling and Resilience

Every layer of the database query stack has its own error handling strategy. `_query_rest_api()` catches `requests.exceptions.RequestException` and inspects response bodies for structured error messages. `_query_llm_for_api()` catches `JSONDecodeError` when the LLM fails to produce valid JSON, and wraps all other exceptions with descriptive messages. `blast_sequence()` implements retry logic with a 10-minute timeout for long-running NCBI BLAST jobs. The NCBI pipeline gracefully handles zero-result searches by returning an empty `formatted_results` array with a `total_results: 0` count, allowing the agent to reason about the absence of data rather than encountering an exception.

This layered error handling means that even if an external API is temporarily unavailable or returns unexpected data, the agent receives a structured error response it can reason about — potentially trying an alternative database or adjusting its query strategy.


# Data Lake Management



Biomni's data lake is the centralized knowledge substrate that grounds every agent interaction in real biological data. Rather than relying solely on LLM parametric memory, the agent reads, retrieves from, and enriches its reasoning with curated local files — from reference ontologies and gene annotation tables to experiment-specific datasets you provide at runtime. This page covers the architecture, lifecycle, and extensibility of that data layer.

## Architecture Overview

The data lake sits at the intersection of three subsystems: the **agent core** that consumes it, the **S3 sync pipeline** that provisions it, and the **runtime extension API** that lets you grow it. Understanding how these connect clarifies every subsequent management operation.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Remote["Remote Sources"]
        S3["S3 Bucket<br/>biomni-release.s3.amazonaws.com"]
        Synapse["Synapse Platform"]
        ProtocolsIO["Protocols.io API"]
    end

    subgraph LocalDataLake["Local Data Lake"]
        direction TB
        DataLakeDir["biomni_data/data_lake/<br/>(curated reference files)"]
        BenchmarkDir["biomni_data/benchmark/<br/>(evaluation data)"]
        CustomData["_custom_data<br/>(user-added datasets)"]
        ProtocolDir["tool/protocols/<br/>addgene/ thermofisher/"]
        KnowHowRes["know_how/resource/<br/>CRISPick links, gRNA seqs"]
    end

    subgraph AgentCore["A1 Agent"]
        Init["__init__()"]
        SysPrompt["_generate_system_prompt()"]
        Retrieval["_prepare_resources_for_retrieval()"]
    end

    subgraph ExtensionAPI["Extension API"]
        AddData["add_data()"]
        RemoveData["remove_custom_data()"]
        DownloadSyn["download_synapse_data()"]
        SearchProto["search_protocols()"]
    end

    S3 -->|"check_and_download_s3_files()"| DataLakeDir
    S3 -->|"benchmark folder zip"| BenchmarkDir
    Synapse -->|"download_synapse_data()"| AgentCore
    ProtocolsIO -->|"search_protocols()"| AgentCore

    DataLakeDir -->|"data_lake_dict"| Init
    Init --> SysPrompt
    CustomData -->|"merged into data_lake_dict"| SysPrompt
    Retrieval -->|"ToolRetriever"| SysPrompt

    AddData --> CustomData
    RemoveData --> CustomData
    DownloadSyn --> AgentCore
    SearchProto --> AgentCore
```

## Storage Layout and Conventions

When the `A1` agent initializes, it creates a standardized directory tree under the configured `path` (defaulting to `./data`). All curated reference files land inside `biomni_data/data_lake/`, while benchmark evaluation data occupies `biomni_data/benchmark/`. The constructor orchestrates both directories and triggers the download pipeline for any missing artifacts [Sources: [a1.py](/biomni/agent/a1.py#L149-L194)].

```
{path}/                              # Configurable via BiomniConfig.path (default: "./data")
└── biomni_data/
    ├── data_lake/                   # Curated reference files (downloaded from S3)
    │   ├── hp.obo                   # HPO ontology for phenotype annotation
    │   ├── gene_annotation.tsv      # Gene reference data
    │   └── ...                      # Additional reference datasets
    ├── benchmark/                   # Evaluation benchmark data
    │   └── hle/                     # HLE benchmark tasks
    └── (agent working files)
```

The **data lake dictionary** (`data_lake_dict`) defined in [env_desc.py](/biomni/env_desc.py#L1-L80) maps each filename to a human-readable description. This dictionary serves two purposes: it drives the automated S3 download check by listing expected files, and it provides the agent with semantic context about what each file contains when generating the system prompt. In commercial mode, the agent switches to [env_desc_cm.py](/biomni/env_desc_cm.py#L1) which filters out datasets restricted to non-commercial use [Sources: [a1.py](/biomni/agent/a1.py#L100-L113)].

## The S3 Sync Pipeline

On initialization, the agent calls `check_and_download_s3_files()` to reconcile local state against the remote S3 bucket. This function implements a **check-then-download** strategy: it iterates through the expected file list, skips files that already exist locally, and downloads only missing artifacts with progress bars. The data lake files are downloaded individually (for selective recovery), while the benchmark folder is distributed as a zip archive and extracted in bulk [Sources: [utils.py](/biomni/utils.py#L921-L1018)].

The sync behavior is controlled by the `expected_data_lake_files` constructor parameter. When set to `None` (the default), it defaults to `list(self.data_lake_dict.keys())` — meaning all files defined in the environment descriptor are synced. Passing an empty list skips the download entirely, which is useful in sandboxed or offline environments where you pre-provision data manually [Sources: [a1.py](/biomni/agent/a1.py#L163-L192)].

> [!TIP]
> The S3 bucket URL (`https://biomni-release.s3.amazonaws.com`) is hardcoded inside `check_and_download_s3_files()` — not in the config class. To point to a private mirror, you would need to modify the call site in `A1.__init__()` at line 169 or override the function itself.

## How the Agent Consumes the Data Lake

The data lake content flows into the agent through the **system prompt**. During `_generate_system_prompt()`, each entry in `data_lake_dict` is formatted as `"{filename}: {description}"` and injected into the prompt so the LLM knows exactly what local files are available and what they contain. This is critical for grounded reasoning: the agent can reference `hp.obo` for HPO term lookups, read gene annotation files for enrichment analysis, or parse custom datasets you provide — all because it was told they exist [Sources: [a1.py](/biomni/agent/a1.py#L996-L1022)].

When retrieval-augmented tool selection is enabled (`use_tool_retriever=True`), the `_prepare_resources_for_retrieval()` method further filters the data lake to surface only the subset relevant to the current user query, reducing prompt length and improving focus [Sources: [a1.py](/biomni/agent/a1.py#L1646-L1654)].

## Runtime Data Management API

Beyond the pre-provisioned files, the `A1` class exposes a full CRUD-style API for managing custom data at runtime. This is the primary mechanism for injecting domain-specific datasets — your own RNA-seq results, patient cohort files, or specialized annotation tables — into the agent's context without modifying the source code.

### Adding Custom Data

The `add_data()` method accepts a dictionary mapping file paths (or filenames) to descriptions. Each entry is registered in both the internal `_custom_data` dictionary and the shared `data_lake_dict`, ensuring it appears in the system prompt on subsequent reconfiguration. The method automatically calls `self.configure()` to regenerate the system prompt with the new data included [Sources: [a1.py](/biomni/agent/a1.py#L676-L721)].

```python
agent = A1(path="./my_project")

# Add custom datasets to the data lake
agent.add_data({
    "rna_seq_results.csv": "Differential expression results from RNA-seq experiment on treated vs control cells",
    "patient_mutations.vcf": "Somatic mutation calls from whole-exome sequencing of 50 cancer patients",
    "custom_pathway_table.tsv": "Curated signaling pathway annotations for breast cancer subtypes"
})

# The agent now knows these files exist and can read them during execution
agent.go("Analyze the top differentially expressed genes in rna_seq_results.csv and cross-reference with patient_mutations.vcf")
```

### Inspecting and Removing Custom Data

Complementary methods provide read and delete operations. `list_custom_data()` returns name-description pairs, `get_custom_data()` retrieves the full metadata (including file path), and `remove_custom_data()` cleanly deletes from both `_custom_data` and `data_lake_dict` [Sources: [a1.py](/biomni/agent/a1.py#L723-L775)].

| Method | Signature | Returns | Notes |
|--------|-----------|---------|-------|
| `list_custom_data()` | `() -> list[tuple]` | List of `(name, description)` pairs | Empty list if none added |
| `get_custom_data()` | `(name: str) -> dict \| None` | `{path, description}` or `None` | Looks up by filename |
| `remove_custom_data()` | `(name: str) -> bool` | `True` if removed, `False` if not found | Removes from both storage dicts |

## Schema Database for API Query Tools

The `biomni/tool/schema_db/` directory holds 35+ pickled API schema files that power the LLM-driven database query tools. Each `.pkl` file contains the structured endpoint documentation for a specific biological database API. When a `query_*` function like `query_uniprot()` receives a natural language prompt, it loads the corresponding schema pickle, injects it into a system template, and asks the LLM to generate the correct API endpoint URL and parameters [Sources: [database.py](/biomni/tool/database.py#L448-L541)].

| Category | Databases |
|----------|-----------|
| **Protein & Structure** | UniProt, PDB, AlphaFold, EMDB, InterPro, STRING |
| **Genomics & Genetics** | Ensembl, ClinVar, dbSNP, gnomAD, GWAS Catalog, UCSC, ENCODE, ReMap, JASPAR |
| **Pathways & Interactions** | KEGG, Reactome, QuickGO, Open Targets, cBioPortal |
| **Chemistry & Drugs** | PubChem, ChEMBL, UniChem, OpenFDA, DailyMed, ClinicalTrials.gov |
| **Phenotype & Ontology** | HPO (via `hp.obo`), Monarch Initiative |
| **Cross-Domain** | GEO, PRIDE, RegulomeDB, IUCN, WoRMS, MPD, Paleobiology, Synapse, GtoPDb |

> [!TIP]
> The schema pickles are loaded at query time (not at agent init), so adding a new database requires: (1) placing a `.pkl` schema file in `schema_db/`, (2) writing a `query_*` function in `database.py` that loads and uses it, and (3) registering the tool description in `tool_description/database.py`. See [Custom Tools and Data](18-custom-tools-and-data) for the full workflow.

## Supplementary Data Sources

Beyond the core data lake, Biomni integrates several supplementary data channels that the agent can access at runtime.

### Synapse Data Download

The `download_synapse_data()` function in [support_tools.py](/biomni/tool/support_tools.py#L199-L250) provides direct access to the Synapse platform for biomedical datasets. It wraps the `synapse` CLI tool and supports downloading files, datasets, folders, and entire projects by entity ID. Authentication requires the `SYNAPSE_AUTH_TOKEN` environment variable. The function automatically installs `synapseclient` if not present and supports recursive folder downloads and link-following [Sources: [support_tools.py](/biomni/tool/support_tools.py#L199-L250)].

### Local Protocol Library

A curated library of laboratory protocols lives in `biomni/tool/protocols/`, organized by source vendor — currently `addgene/` and `thermofisher/`. These are plain-text protocol files the agent can read directly via `read_local_protocol()`, which searches by filename across all source directories. The companion `list_local_protocols()` function provides a directory listing with filtering by source. This is entirely local (no API calls) and serves as a reference library for wet-lab procedures [Sources: [protocols.py](/biomni/tool/protocols.py#L173-L305)].

### Know-How Resources

The `biomni/know_how/resource/` directory stores supplementary reference materials used by the know-how system — such as CRISPick download links and Addgene gRNA sequence tables. These resources are referenced by the markdown know-how documents and loaded through the `KnowHowLoader` class, providing the agent with actionable reference data for specific experimental workflows [Sources: [loader.py](/biomni/know_how/loader.py#L8-L349)].

### BLAST Sequence Search

The `blast_sequence()` function in [database.py](/biomni/tool/database.py#L2852-L2953) submits sequences to the NCBI BLAST web service, bridging local sequence data with remote homology databases. Combined with the local data lake files, this enables end-to-end workflows where the agent reads a sequence from a local file and blasts it against NCBI's curated databases.

## Academic vs Commercial Data Filtering

The `commercial_mode` configuration flag (set via `BiomniConfig.commercial_mode` or the `A1` constructor) controls which data files the agent is allowed to reference. In **academic mode** (default, `False`), all datasets in `env_desc.py` are available. In **commercial mode** (`True`), the agent switches to `env_desc_cm.py`, which excludes datasets with non-commercial licensing restrictions. This filtering applies to both the data lake dictionary and the know-how documents — the `_filter_know_how_for_commercial_mode()` method removes know-how entries that carry commercial use restrictions when this mode is active [Sources: [a1.py](/biomni/agent/a1.py#L100-L113), [a1.py](/biomni/agent/a1.py#L876-L882)].

| Setting | Data Lake Source | Know-How Filtering | Use Case |
|----------|-----------------|-------------------|----------|
| `commercial_mode=False` | `env_desc.py` (all datasets) | None — all documents loaded | Academic research, personal projects |
| `commercial_mode=True` | `env_desc_cm.py` (licensed only) | Removes non-commercial documents | Industry applications, commercial products |

## Configuration Reference

Data lake management is governed by two configuration touchpoints: the `BiomniConfig` dataclass and the `A1` constructor parameters. Environment variable overrides are supported for CI/CD and containerized deployments.

| Parameter | Config Key | Env Variable | Default | Description |
|-----------|-----------|--------------|---------|-------------|
| `path` | `BiomniConfig.path` | `BIOMNI_PATH` / `BIOMNI_DATA_PATH` | `"./data"` | Root directory for data lake and benchmark files |
| `commercial_mode` | `BiomniConfig.commercial_mode` | `BIOMNI_COMMERCIAL_MODE` | `False` | Exclude non-commercial datasets |
| `timeout_seconds` | `BiomniConfig.timeout_seconds` | `BIOMNI_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` | `600` | Timeout for code execution (affects file I/O operations) |
| `expected_data_lake_files` | (constructor only) | — | `None` (all files) | Explicit file list; empty list skips download |
| `protocols_io_access_token` | `BiomniConfig.protocols_io_access_token` | `PROTOCOLS_IO_ACCESS_TOKEN` | `None` | Token for protocols.io API access |

Sources: [config.py](/biomni/config.py#L12-L99)

## Practical Walkthrough

The following flowchart illustrates the complete lifecycle of data lake management from first initialization through runtime extension.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["agent = A1(path='./my_lab')"] --> B{"Directory exists?"}
    B -->|No| C["Create ./my_lab/biomni_data/"]
    B -->|Yes| D["Scan existing files"]
    C --> D
    D --> E{"expected_data_lake_files<br/>is None?"}
    E -->|Yes| F["Load data_lake_dict keys<br/>as expected file list"]
    E -->|No, empty list| G["Skip download"]
    F --> H["check_and_download_s3_files()<br/>Sync missing data lake files"]
    H --> I{"commercial_mode?"}
    G --> I
    I -->|True| J["Load env_desc_cm.py<br/>(licensed datasets only)"]
    I -->|False| K["Load env_desc.py<br/>(all datasets)"]
    J --> L["Initialize KnowHowLoader<br/>Filter non-commercial docs"]
    K --> M["Initialize KnowHowLoader<br/>(all documents)"]
    L --> N["agent.add_data({custom files})"]
    M --> N
    N --> O["configure() → Regenerate system prompt<br/>with data lake + custom data"]
    O --> P["agent.go(query)<br/>Agent reads and reasons<br/>over all available data"]
```

- **[Know-How Library](17-know-how-library)** — How markdown-based expert knowledge complements the structured data lake.
- **[Custom Tools and Data](18-custom-tools-and-data)** — End-to-end guide for adding new data files, schema pickles, and query functions.
