# Know-How Library



The Know-How Library is Biomni's mechanism for injecting curated domain expertise directly into the agent's reasoning context. Unlike tools that the agent *calls* and data it *reads*, know-how documents are **already-loaded reference materials** — expert protocols, best-practice guides, and troubleshooting references that the agent can cite and follow without any retrieval overhead. This page covers the loader architecture, document authoring conventions, retrieval integration, and how to extend the library with your own domain knowledge.

## Architectural Overview

The Know-How Library sits at the intersection of the knowledge layer and the agent's system prompt. Documents are authored as structured Markdown files, parsed by the `KnowHowLoader` class, filtered by licensing constraints, and selectively injected into the agent's context through the retrieval pipeline. The design intentionally separates *metadata* (used for selection and display) from *content* (used for reasoning), ensuring the agent receives clean, actionable guidance.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph "Authoring Layer"
        MD["Markdown Documents<br/>(.md files)"]
        RES["Resource Files<br/>(CSV, TXT)"]
    end

    subgraph "KnowHowLoader"
        LOAD["_load_documents()"]
        META["_extract_metadata()"]
        STRIP["_strip_metadata()"]
    end

    subgraph "Agent Integration"
        INIT["A1.__init__()"]
        FILTER["_filter_know_how_for_commercial_mode()"]
        RETRIEVE["_prepare_resources_for_retrieval()"]
        PROMPT["_generate_system_prompt()"]
    end

    subgraph "Runtime"
        RETRIEVER["ToolRetriever<br/>(prompt-based selection)"]
        LLM["Agent LLM"]
    end

    MD --> LOAD --> META
    LOAD --> STRIP
    INIT --> FILTER
    INIT --> LOAD
    RETRIEVE --> RETRIEVER
    RETRIEVE --> PROMPT
    PROMPT --> LLM

    style MD fill:#e8f5e9
    style LLM fill:#fff3e0
    style RETRIEVER fill:#e3f2fd
```

## The KnowHowLoader Class

The `KnowHowLoader` class ([loader.py](biomni/know_how/loader.py#L8-L349)) is the sole entry point exposed by the `biomni.know_how` module ([\_\_init\_\_.py](biomni/know_how/__init__.py#L7-L9)). It is exported as `__all__ = ["KnowHowLoader"]` and instantiated automatically by the A1 agent during initialization.

### Initialization and Document Discovery

On construction, the loader resolves the know-how directory to the package's own `know_how/` folder by default, then immediately loads all qualifying Markdown files.

```python
def __init__(self, know_how_dir: str | None = None):
    if know_how_dir is None:
        current_dir = Path(__file__).parent
        know_how_dir = str(current_dir)
    self.know_how_dir = know_how_dir
    self.documents = {}
    self._load_documents()
```

Sources: [loader.py](biomni/know_how/loader.py#L11-L26)

The `_load_documents()` method scans the directory with a `*.md` glob pattern. It intentionally skips meta-files — any Markdown whose filename (without extension) is entirely uppercase (e.g., `README.md`, `QUICK_START.md`) is excluded. This convention allows you to place project documentation like READMEs in the same directory without them being treated as know-how content.

Sources: [loader.py](biomni/know_how/loader.py#L28-L62)

### Metadata Extraction

Each document follows a structured format. The loader extracts three categories of information through `_extract_metadata()`:

| Extracted Field | Source | Fallback |
|---|---|---|
| **Title** | First `# H1` heading in the document | Filename, title-cased with underscores replaced by spaces |
| **Description** | Content under `## Overview` section, truncated to 200 characters; overridden by `**Short Description**` from metadata if present | First non-empty paragraph after the title |
| **Metadata dict** | Key-value pairs from the `## Metadata` section (e.g., Authors, Version, License, Commercial Use) | Empty dict |

The metadata parser recognizes a `**FieldName**:` pattern at the start of lines and captures list items (`- `) as comma-separated values within a single field. This flexible approach supports multi-line metadata entries without requiring strict YAML frontmatter.

Sources: [loader.py](biomni/know_how/loader.py#L64-L163)

### Content Stripping

Before know-how content reaches the agent, the `_strip_metadata()` method removes the entire `## Metadata` section and any surrounding horizontal rule separators. The result — stored as `content_without_metadata` on each document — is what the agent actually sees in its system prompt. This keeps the reasoning context lean and focused on actionable guidance rather than administrative metadata.

Sources: [loader.py](biomni/know_how/loader.py#L165-L224)

### Document Management API

The loader provides a full CRUD surface for managing documents at runtime:

| Method | Purpose | Returns |
|---|---|---|
| `get_all_documents()` | Retrieve every loaded document with full content | `list[dict]` |
| `get_document_by_id(doc_id)` | Look up a single document by its filename stem | `dict \| None` |
| `get_document_summaries()` | Lightweight list with only id, name, description | `list[dict]` |
| `get_document_metadata(doc_id)` | Access only the parsed metadata dict | `dict \| None` |
| `add_custom_document(doc_id, name, description, content, metadata)` | Programmatically inject a document (no file on disk) | `None` |
| `remove_document(doc_id)` | Delete from the in-memory store | `None` |
| `reload()` | Re-scan the directory from disk, discarding all in-memory changes | `None` |
| `print_document_info(doc_id)` | Pretty-print document details including metadata to stdout | `None` |

Sources: [loader.py](biomni/know_how/loader.py#L226-L349)

> [!TIP]
> **Programmatic vs. File-based documents**: Documents added via `add_custom_document()` exist only in memory and will not survive a `reload()` call. If you need persistent custom know-how, either place a properly structured `.md` file in the know-how directory and call `reload()`, or re-add the document after each reload.

## Bundled Know-How Documents

The repository ships with two expert-level guides that demonstrate the full document format, plus companion resource files.

### sgRNA Design Guide

**File**: [sgRNA_design_guide.md](biomni/know_how/sgRNA_design_guide.md) · **Resource**: [addgene_grna_sequences.csv](biomni/know_how/resource/addgene_grna_sequences.csv), [CRISPick_download_links.txt](biomni/know_how/resource/CRISPick_download_links.txt)

This 420-line guide implements a **three-tiered approach** to CRISPR guide RNA design, prioritizing experimentally validated sequences over computational predictions:

1. **Option 1 — Validated Sequences** (recommended first): Search a curated database of 300+ validated sgRNAs sourced from Addgene, with mandatory cross-referencing via web literature search.
2. **Option 2 — CRISPick Pre-Computed Designs**: Download and filter pre-scored sgRNA datasets from the Broad Institute's CRISPick tool, including a complete download URL registry in the companion text file.
3. **Option 3 — De Novo Design Guidelines** (last resort): General rules for on-target efficiency, PAM compatibility, and off-target minimization when no pre-existing data is available.

The guide includes reproducible Python code snippets, a database column reference, citation requirements for both Addgene and CRISPick sources, and quick-start walkthroughs for common tasks (e.g., knocking out TP53, activating OCT4).

Sources: [sgRNA_design_guide.md](biomni/know_how/sgRNA_design_guide.md#L1-L100), [sgRNA_design_guide.md](biomni/know_how/sgRNA_design_guide.md#L146-L420)

### Single Cell RNA-seq Annotation

**File**: [single_cell_annotation.md](biomni/know_how/single_cell_annotation.md)

This 224-page guide distills best practices from the "Single-cell best practices" reference by Luecken, Theis, et al. It covers three complementary annotation strategies:

| Approach | Method | Recommended For |
|---|---|---|
| Manual Marker-Based | Cluster-wise differential expression against known markers | Small datasets, novel cell types |
| Automated | Pre-trained classifiers (CellTypist, scAnnotate) | Standard tissues, large-scale screening |
| Reference-Based Transfer | Label transfer from annotated atlases (scArches, Azimuth, SingleR) | Well-characterized tissues, cross-study integration |

The guide provides a four-step recommended workflow (QC → manual assessment → automated validation → reference refinement), a tool selection matrix keyed to scenario, key marker gene tables by cell lineage (blood/immune, epithelial, stromal), a validation checklist, and a troubleshooting section covering common pitfalls like doublet clusters, ambient RNA contamination, and reference mismatch.

Sources: [single_cell_annotation.md](biomni/know_how/single_cell_annotation.md#L27-L224)

### Resource Files

The `biomni/know_how/resource/` directory contains companion data files referenced by know-how documents:

| File | Purpose | Referenced By |
|---|---|---|
| `addgene_grna_sequences.csv` | Curated database of 300+ validated sgRNA sequences with PubMed IDs, plasmid links, and species/application metadata | sgRNA Design Guide Option 1 |
| `CRISPick_download_links.txt` | Registry of download URLs for pre-computed CRISPick sgRNA design files | sgRNA Design Guide Option 2 |

These files are static assets — the know-how guides instruct the agent on how to programmatically load and query them using `pandas` or `advanced_web_search_claude`.

## Integration with the Agent Pipeline

The Know-How Library is wired into the A1 agent at three critical junctures: initialization, retrieval selection, and system prompt injection.

### Initialization and Commercial Filtering

When the A1 agent is constructed, it instantiates `KnowHowLoader()` with the default directory ([a1.py](biomni/agent/a1.py#L212-L213)). If `commercial_mode=True`, the agent immediately calls `_filter_know_how_for_commercial_mode()` ([a1.py](biomni/agent/a1.py#L876-L896)), which scans every document's metadata for commercial use restrictions — specifically looking for ❌ symbols, "Not Allowed", or "Non-Commercial" in the `commercial_use` field — and removes any restricted documents from the in-memory store. Both bundled documents carry `Commercial Use: ✅ Allowed` in their metadata, so they survive this filter.

Sources: [a1.py](biomni/agent/a1.py#L212-L219), [a1.py](biomni/agent/a1.py#L876-L896)

### Retrieval-Augmented Selection

When tool retrieval is enabled (`use_tool_retriever=True`), the `_prepare_resources_for_retrieval()` method ([a1.py](biomni/agent/a1.py#L1646-L1757)) gathers know-how document summaries (id, name, description only) alongside tools, data lake items, and libraries into a unified resource dictionary. This entire set is passed to the `ToolRetriever.prompt_based_retrieval()` method, which asks the agent's LLM to select the most relevant resources for the current query.

For any know-how documents that the retriever selects, the pipeline fetches the **full stripped content** via `get_document_by_id()` and uses `content_without_metadata` — not the raw content — for the agent context. This two-stage approach means the LLM makes selection decisions from lightweight summaries while receiving complete, actionable content for reasoning.

Sources: [a1.py](biomni/agent/a1.py#L1690-L1746)

### System Prompt Injection

The `_generate_system_prompt()` method ([a1.py](biomni/agent/a1.py#L1087-L1186)) formats selected know-how documents into a dedicated `📚 KNOW-HOW DOCUMENTS` section placed at the top of the system prompt under `PRIORITY CUSTOM RESOURCES`. The prompt explicitly instructs the agent:

> These documents are ALREADY AVAILABLE in your context. You do NOT need to retrieve them or "review" them as a separate step. You can DIRECTLY reference and use the information from these documents.

This is a critical design decision — know-how content is not something the agent must *search for* or *load*. It is already present in the system prompt, and the agent is expected to reference it directly when answering questions, generating protocols, suggesting parameters, or providing troubleshooting guidance.

Sources: [a1.py](biomni/agent/a1.py#L1173-L1186)

## Authoring Custom Know-How Documents

You can extend the library by authoring new Markdown files following the established conventions. The loader is deliberately tolerant of format variations, but adhering to the standard structure ensures correct metadata extraction, proper retrieval behavior, and clean agent context.

### Required Structure

Every know-how document must follow this skeleton:

```markdown
# Your Document Title

---

## Metadata

**Short Description**: A concise one-line summary (used by the retriever for selection decisions).

**Authors**: Author or team name

**Version**: 1.0

**Last Updated**: Month Year

**License**: CC BY 4.0

**Commercial Use**: ✅ Allowed   <!-- or ❌ Not Allowed -->

---

## Overview

This paragraph becomes the document's description field. Keep it focused and informative —
the retriever uses this text to decide whether the document is relevant to a query.

## Your Content Sections

The actual guidance, protocols, code examples, tables, and troubleshooting steps go here.
All of this content (minus the Metadata section) is what the agent sees in its context.
```

### File Placement and Naming Conventions

| Convention | Rule | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Location** | Place in `biomni/know_how/` directory | `biomni/know_how/flow_cytometry_guide.md` |
| **Filename** | Must be `.md`; must NOT be all-uppercase (those are skipped) | ✅ `flow_cytometry.md` · ❌ `README.md` · ❌ `GUIDE_V2.MD` |
| **Title** | First `# H1` heading | `# Flow Cytometry Panel Design` |
| **Metadata section** | Must be `## Metadata` (case-sensitive) | Required for proper extraction |
| **Overview section** | Must be `## Overview` (case-sensitive) | Used as description fallback |

> [!TIP]
> **Retrieval relevance depends on your Overview and Short Description**: The retriever selects know-how documents based on their summaries (name + description). Write a `Short Description` that includes the key terms a user might mention in their query — tool names, technique names, organism types, and experimental contexts all improve selection accuracy.

### Adding Documents Programmatically

For documents that should exist only within a session (or that are generated dynamically), use the loader's `add_custom_document()` method:

```python
from biomni.know_how import KnowHowLoader

loader = KnowHowLoader()

loader.add_custom_document(
    doc_id="custom_protocol",
    name="Custom Western Blot Protocol",
    description="Step-by-step Western blot protocol for membrane protein detection",
    content="""
## Materials
- PVDF membrane, blocking buffer...

## Procedure
1. Transfer proteins to PVDF membrane...
""",
    metadata={
        "authors": "Your Lab",
        "version": "1.0",
        "commercial_use": "✅ Allowed"
    }
)

# Verify it loaded
loader.print_document_info("custom_protocol")
```

Note that programmatically added documents will not have a `content_without_metadata` field unless you separately strip metadata from the content before passing it. The `_strip_metadata()` method operates on the `## Metadata` section format — if your custom content doesn't include one, the full content is used as-is.

Sources: [loader.py](biomni/know_how/loader.py#L258-L279), [loader.py](biomni/know_how/loader.py#L53-L62)

## End-to-End Data Flow

The following sequence traces a know-how document from authoring through to agent consumption:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Author as Document Author
    participant Loader as KnowHowLoader
    participant Agent as A1 Agent
    participant Retriever as ToolRetriever
    participant LLM as Agent LLM

    Author->>Loader: Place .md in know_how/
    Loader->>Loader: "_load_documents() scans *.md"
    Loader->>Loader: "_extract_metadata() → title, description, metadata dict"
    Loader->>Loader: "_strip_metadata() → content_without_metadata"
    Loader-->>Agent: know_how_loader.documents populated
    Agent->>Agent: "_filter_know_how_for_commercial_mode()"
    Agent->>Retriever: "get_document_summaries() for selection"
    Retriever->>LLM: "Which know-how docs match this query?"
    LLM-->>Retriever: Selected doc IDs
    Retriever-->>Agent: Selected document IDs
    Agent->>Loader: "get_document_by_id(doc_id)"
    Loader-->>Agent: Full doc with content_without_metadata
    Agent->>Agent: "_generate_system_prompt() injects 📚 section"
    Agent->>LLM: System prompt with know-how content
    LLM->>LLM: Reasons using embedded expertise
```

## Relationship to Other Resource Layers

The Know-How Library is one of four resource categories the A1 agent can draw upon. Understanding its position in this ecosystem clarifies when to use know-how versus other extension mechanisms:

| Resource Layer | Injection Method | Agent Access Pattern | Typical Content |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Know-How** | Embedded in system prompt (full content) | Direct reference, no retrieval step | Best practices, protocols, troubleshooting |
| **Custom Tools** | Listed in system prompt + importable | `from module import function` | New Python functions, API wrappers |
| **Custom Data** | Listed in system prompt + file path | Read from data lake directory | Datasets, reference files |
| **Custom Software** | Listed in system prompt + importable | `import library` | Additional Python packages |

The key distinction: know-how documents change *what the agent knows*, while tools change *what the agent can do*, data changes *what the agent can read*, and software changes *what the agent can compute with*. For deeper exploration of these complementary systems, see [Tool Registry and Discovery](12-tool-registry-and-discovery), [Data Lake Management](16-data-lake-management), and [Retrieval-Augmented Tool Selection](13-retrieval-augmented-tool-selection).

# Custom Tools and Data



Biomni's extensibility model is built around three distinct resource types — **tools** (callable functions), **data** (files in the data lake), and **software** (CLI/library entries) — each managed through a dedicated CRUD API on the `A1` agent instance. When you add any custom resource, the agent automatically reconfigures its system prompt to surface your additions as **priority resources**, visually distinguished with emoji markers and an explicit directive to use them first. This page covers the full lifecycle: authoring, registering, querying, and removing custom resources, along with the know-how document system for embedding domain expertise directly into the agent's context.

## Architecture Overview

Every custom resource flows through the same general pipeline: registration into an internal data structure, propagation into the system prompt, and exposure to the LLM at inference time. The diagram below shows how the three resource types converge on system prompt generation during `configure()`.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Input
        FT["Custom Function"]
        FD["Custom Data File"]
        FS["Custom Software"]
        FH["Know-How .md"]
    end

    subgraph A1_Agent["A1 Agent"]
        direction TB
        AT["add_tool()"]
        AD["add_data()"]
        AS["add_software()"]
        AH["add_custom_document()"]
        CONF["configure()"]
        PROMPT["_generate_system_prompt()"]
    end

    subgraph Internal
        TR["ToolRegistry"]
        M2A["module2api"]
        DLD["data_lake_dict"]
        LCD["library_content_dict"]
        KHL["KnowHowLoader.documents"]
    end

    FT --> AT --> TR & M2A
    FD --> AD --> DLD
    FS --> AS --> LCD
    FH --> AH --> KHL

    TR & M2A & DLD & LCD & KHL --> CONF --> PROMPT
```

The critical design decision is that all three resource types are **shallowly merged** into their respective master dictionaries (`data_lake_dict`, `library_content_dict`) while also tracked separately in `_custom_data`, `_custom_software`, and `_custom_tools` maps. This dual-tracking allows the system prompt generator to separate custom from default resources and render custom items with special formatting and priority instructions.

Sources: [a1.py](biomni/agent/a1.py#L1289-L1378), [tool_registry.py](biomni/tool/tool_registry.py#L6-L18)

## Adding Custom Tools

Custom tools are Python functions that the agent can call during its reasoning loop. The `add_tool()` method accepts any callable and performs full schema introspection, registration, and injection in a single call.

### The Registration Pipeline

When you call `agent.add_tool(my_function)`, the following sequence executes:

1. **Source inspection**: `inspect.getsource(api)` extracts the function's source code from its module.
2. **Schema generation**: The source code is passed to `function_to_api_schema(function_code, self.llm)` which uses the configured LLM to produce a structured schema dictionary. This schema must contain `name`, `description`, and `required_parameters` to pass validation.
3. **Registry insertion**: The schema is registered into `ToolRegistry` via `register_tool()`, which assigns an auto-incrementing integer `id` and appends it to the tools list. The registry's `document_df` DataFrame is then rebuilt to include the new tool for retrieval-augmented tool selection.
4. **Module mapping**: The schema is added to `module2api[module_name]`, keyed by the function's `__module__` attribute (defaulting to `"custom_tools"`). Duplicate tool names within the same module are updated in-place rather than duplicated.
5. **REPL injection**: The original callable is stored in `builtins._biomni_custom_functions[name]` so the Python REPL execution environment can invoke it directly via `_inject_custom_functions_to_repl()`.
6. **Agent reconfiguration**: `self.configure()` is called to regenerate the system prompt with the new tool surfaced as a priority resource.

Sources: [a1.py](biomni/agent/a1.py#L225-L348)

### Authoring Requirements

Your custom function should be a well-documented Python callable. The LLM-based schema generator relies on the function signature, docstring, and type annotations to produce accurate parameter descriptions. Here is a minimal example:

```python
# before: no tool available
def calculate_gc_content(dna_sequence: str) -> str:
    """Calculate GC content percentage of a DNA sequence.
    
    Args:
        dna_sequence: A string of nucleotide characters (A, T, G, C)
        
    Returns:
        GC content as a percentage string
    """
    gc = dna_sequence.upper().count('G') + dna_sequence.upper().count('C')
    total = len(dna_sequence)
    return f"GC content: {(gc / total * 100):.2f}%"

agent.add_tool(calculate_gc_content)
```

| Requirement | Detail |
|---|---|
| Callable | Must be a Python function or callable object |
| Docstring | Used by the LLM schema generator; include parameter descriptions |
| Type hints | Annotated types guide schema generation accuracy |
| Return value | Should be a string or JSON-serializable for the REPL to display |

> [!TIP]
> The `function_to_api_schema()` call in `add_tool()` is **asynchronous in nature** — it invokes the configured LLM to parse your function. If your LLM is misconfigured or returns malformed output, the method raises a `ValueError`. Always verify your LLM connection before adding tools.

### Managing Custom Tools at Runtime

The `A1` class exposes a full CRUD interface for custom tools after registration:

| Method | Signature | Returns |
|---|---|---|
| `add_tool` | `add_tool(api: Callable) -> dict` | The generated schema |
| `list_custom_tools` | `list_custom_tools() -> list` | List of custom tool names |
| `get_custom_tool` | `get_custom_tool(name: str) -> dict \| None` | Tool metadata or `None` |
| `remove_custom_tool` | `remove_custom_tool(name: str) -> bool` | Success flag |

Removing a tool clears it from `_custom_tools`, `module2api`, and `_custom_functions` (the REPL injection namespace), then reconfigures the agent. Note that removal from the `ToolRegistry`'s internal `tools` list is not performed — only the custom tracking maps are cleaned. If you need full registry removal, use `tool_registry.remove_tool_by_name()` directly.

Sources: [a1.py](biomni/agent/a1.py#L589-L674)

## Adding Custom Data

The data lake is Biomni's file-level context system. It tells the agent which files exist and what they contain so the LLM can reason about which data to load. The `add_data()` method lets you register your own files alongside the default data lake contents.

### Registration

```python
agent.add_data({
    "path/to/my_experiment.csv": "Single-cell RNA-seq counts from patient tumor biopsy",
    "results/blast_hits.fasta": "BLAST alignment results against NCBI nr database"
})
```

Internally, the method iterates over the dictionary, extracts the basename from each path for storage, and populates two structures simultaneously: `_custom_data[filename]` with `{"path": ..., "description": ...}`, and `data_lake_dict[filename]` with the description string. This ensures the file appears in both the custom tracking layer and the master data lake dictionary used by the system prompt generator. After insertion, `self.configure()` is called automatically.

Sources: [a1.py](biomni/agent/a1.py#L676-L721)

### CRUD Interface for Data

| Method | Signature | Returns |
|---|---|---|
| `add_data` | `add_data(data: dict) -> bool` | Success flag |
| `list_custom_data` | `list_custom_data() -> list` | `[(name, description), ...]` |
| `get_custom_data` | `get_custom_data(name: str) -> dict \| None` | `{path, description}` or `None` |
| `remove_custom_data` | `remove_custom_data(name: str) -> bool` | Success flag |

> [!TIP]
> The `add_data()` method does **not** copy files — it only registers paths. The files must already exist at the specified locations when the agent attempts to access them during execution.

Sources: [a1.py](biomni/agent/a1.py#L723-L775)

## Adding Custom Software

Software entries represent CLI tools, R packages, or Python libraries installed in the environment that the agent can invoke via Bash, R, or Python execution blocks. The `add_software()` method follows the same dual-tracking pattern as data.

### Registration

```python
agent.add_software({
    "plink2": "Genome-wide association study analysis toolset",
    "cellranger": "10x Genomics single-cell RNA-seq processing pipeline"
})
```

The method validates that the input is a dictionary with string keys and values, stores each entry in `_custom_software[software_name]` with `{name, description}`, and mirrors it into `library_content_dict[software_name]` for system prompt generation. It then calls `self.configure()`.

Sources: [a1.py](biomni/agent/a1.py#L777-L820)

### CRUD Interface for Software

| Method | Signature | Returns |
|---|---|---|
| `add_software` | `add_software(software: dict) -> bool` | Success flag |
| `list_custom_software` | `list_custom_software() -> list` | `[(name, description), ...]` |
| `get_custom_software` | `get_custom_software(name: str) -> dict \| None` | `{name, description}` or `None` |
| `remove_custom_software` | `remove_custom_software(name: str) -> bool` | Success flag |

Sources: [a1.py](biomni/agent/a1.py#L822-L875)

## How Custom Resources Appear in the System Prompt

When any custom resources exist, the `_generate_system_prompt()` method inserts a **PRIORITY CUSTOM RESOURCES** section at the top of the prompt, before the default tools, data lake, and software listings. Each resource type receives a distinct emoji prefix and formatting:

| Resource Type | Prefix | Format |
|---|---|---|
| Custom tools | 🔧 | `🔧 tool_name (from module): description` |
| Custom data | 📊 | `📊 filename: description` |
| Custom software | ⚙️ | `⚙️ software_name: description` |
| Know-how docs | 📚 | `📚 doc_name:\n full_content` |

The prompt includes an explicit directive: *"PRIORITIZE using these resources as they are directly relevant to your task. Always consider these FIRST and in the meantime using default resources."* This ensures the LLM treats your additions as first-class resources rather than afterthoughts. Default resources are listed separately below, filtered to exclude any items already present in the custom lists to avoid duplication.

Sources: [a1.py](biomni/agent/a1.py#L1053-L1199)

## Know-How Documents

The know-how system provides a fourth extensibility channel specifically for **procedural knowledge** — best practices, protocols, parameter recommendations, and troubleshooting guides. Unlike tools (which are executable), know-how documents are markdown files injected verbatim into the system prompt as reference material.

### How Documents Are Loaded

The `KnowHowLoader` class scans the `biomni/know_how/` directory for `.md` files on initialization. It skips meta-documents (filenames that are all uppercase, like `README.md`) and processes each file through a metadata extraction pipeline:

1. **Title extraction**: The first `# H1` heading is used; falls back to a title-cased filename.
2. **Metadata parsing**: Content under `## Metadata` is parsed for `**Field**:` patterns (e.g., `**Authors**:`, `**Topics**:`, `**License**:`) into a structured dictionary.
3. **Description extraction**: Content under `## Overview` (up to 200 characters) is used; falls back to the first non-empty paragraph after the title.
4. **Content stripping**: The `_strip_metadata()` method removes the metadata section from the full content, producing `content_without_metadata` that is used in system prompts.

Sources: [loader.py](biomni/know_how/loader.py#L8-L163)

### Document Metadata Format

The expected markdown structure for a know-how document is:

```markdown
# Document Title

## Metadata
**Authors**: Research team name
**Topics**: CRISPR, guide RNA design, off-target analysis
**License**: MIT

## Overview
Brief description of what this document covers and when to reference it.

## Detailed Content
Full procedural content, parameters, troubleshooting steps, etc.
```

Key metadata fields recognized by the loader include `short_description` (overrides the extracted overview), `authors`, `topics`, and `license`. The `license` field is particularly important — when the agent runs in **commercial mode**, documents with non-commercial license restrictions are filtered out by `_filter_know_how_for_commercial_mode()`.

Sources: [loader.py](biomni/know_how/loader.py#L28-L62), [a1.py](biomni/agent/a1.py#L876-L896)

### Adding Custom Know-How Documents at Runtime

You can add know-how documents programmatically without placing files on disk:

```python
agent.know_how_loader.add_custom_document(
    doc_id="my_protocol",
    name="Custom Western Blot Protocol",
    description="Step-by-step western blot with ECL detection",
    content="# Custom Western Blot\n## Steps\n1. Prepare samples...\n2. Run SDS-PAGE...",
    metadata={"authors": "Lab Team", "topics": "western blot, protein detection"}
)
agent.configure()  # Reconfigure to pick up new know-how
```

The `add_custom_document()` method stores the document in the same structure as disk-loaded documents. The method also supports a `metadata` dictionary argument for programmatic metadata injection. After adding, call `agent.configure()` to regenerate the system prompt with the new document included.

| Method | Signature | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `add_custom_document` | `add_custom_document(doc_id, name, description, content, metadata=None)` | Register a new document |
| `get_all_documents` | `get_all_documents() -> list[dict]` | List all loaded documents |
| `get_document_by_id` | `get_document_by_id(doc_id) -> dict \| None` | Retrieve specific document |
| `get_document_summaries` | `get_document_summaries() -> list[dict]` | List documents without full content |
| `remove_document` | `remove_document(doc_id)` | Remove a document |
| `reload` | `reload()` | Re-scan the know-how directory from disk |

Sources: [loader.py](biomni/know_how/loader.py#L258-L347)

## Built-in Know-How Resources

The repository ships with two default know-how documents in the `biomni/know_how/` directory, each accompanied by reference resource files in `biomni/know_how/resource/`:

| Document | Resource Files | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `sgRNA_design_guide.md` | `CRISPick_download_links.txt`, `addgene_grna_sequences.csv` | Expert guidance on single guide RNA design for CRISPR experiments |
| `single_cell_annotation.md` | — | Best practices for single-cell RNA-seq cell type annotation |

These documents are loaded automatically during agent initialization and included in full (metadata-stripped) in the initial system prompt. In commercial mode, any know-how document with a non-commercial license is excluded via the `_filter_know_how_for_commercial_mode()` method.

Sources: [loader.py](biomni/know_how/loader.py#L19-L26), [a1.py](biomni/agent/a1.py#L212-L219)

## Tool Registry Internals

The `ToolRegistry` class is the low-level storage engine for all tools (both built-in and custom). Understanding its validation rules is essential if you bypass `add_tool()` and construct schemas manually.

### Validation Contract

Every tool must be a dictionary containing these three keys:

| Required Key | Type | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | `str` | Unique tool identifier used for lookup and REPL invocation |
| `description` | `str` | Human-readable description for LLM reasoning and retrieval |
| `required_parameters` | `list` | Array of parameter definitions consumed by the LLM |

Optional keys include `optional_parameters`, `module` (source module name), and `id` (auto-assigned integer). The `validate_tool()` method raises `ValueError` on missing required keys.

### Registry Operations

The registry supports bidirectional lookup by name or ID, persistence via `save_registry()`/`load_registry()` (using Python pickle), and removal by either identifier. When `add_tool()` adds a new tool, it also rebuilds the `document_df` DataFrame — a two-column DataFrame of `[docid, document_content]` used by the retrieval-augmented tool selection system.

Sources: [tool_registry.py](biomni/tool/tool_registry.py#L24-L89)

## Quick Reference: Complete Customization Workflow

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Define custom function"] --> B["agent.add_tool(func)"]
    C["Prepare data files"] --> D["agent.add_data({path: desc})"]
    E["Install CLI software"] --> F["agent.add_software({name: desc})"]
    G["Write know-how .md"] --> H["agent.know_how_loader.add_custom_document(...)"]

    B --> I["agent.configure()"]
    D --> I
    F --> I
    H --> I

    I --> J["System prompt includes\n🔧📊⚙️📚 priority resources"]
    J --> K["agent.go(prompt)"]
```

| Action | Method | Triggers Reconfigure |
|---|---|---|
| Add tool | `agent.add_tool(func)` | ✅ Automatic |
| Remove tool | `agent.remove_custom_tool(name)` | ❌ Manual |
| Add data | `agent.add_data({path: desc})` | ✅ Automatic |
| Remove data | `agent.remove_custom_data(name)` | ❌ Manual |
| Add software | `agent.add_software({name: desc})` | ✅ Automatic |
| Remove software | `agent.remove_custom_software(name)` | ❌ Manual |
| Add know-how | `agent.know_how_loader.add_custom_document(...)` | ❌ Manual |
| Remove know-how | `agent.know_how_loader.remove_document(id)` | ❌ Manual |

For removal operations that do not auto-reconfigure, you must call `agent.configure()` explicitly to regenerate the system prompt and pick up the changes.

---

For integration with external tool servers via the Model Context Protocol, see [MCP Server Integration](19-mcp-server-integration). To understand how tools are discovered at runtime through retrieval, refer to [Retrieval-Augmented Tool Selection](13-retrieval-augmented-tool-selection). For the full tool schema format used by built-in tools, consult [Domain Tool Implementations](14-domain-tool-implementations).

# MCP Server Integration



Biomni's MCP (Model Context Protocol) integration provides a bidirectional bridge between its internal tool ecosystem and the broader MCP ecosystem. This dual-mode architecture lets you import tools from any MCP-compatible server into Biomni's agent workflow, and conversely, expose Biomni's native domain tools as MCP servers consumable by external AI clients. The implementation lives primarily in the [`A1`](biomni/agent/a1.py#L56) agent class, with two complementary methods — [`add_mcp()`](biomni/agent/a1.py#L350) for inbound tool ingestion and [`create_mcp_server()`](biomni/agent/a1.py#L1995) for outbound tool exposure.

Sources: [a1.py](biomni/agent/a1.py#L56-L56), [mcp_integration.md](docs/mcp_integration.md#L1-L11)

## Architectural Overview

The MCP integration layer operates at the boundary between Biomni's synchronous agent execution model and the inherently asynchronous MCP protocol. All communication with external MCP servers uses the **stdio transport** — servers are spawned as child processes, and tools are invoked through structured message passing over stdin/stdout. This architecture avoids network complexity while maintaining isolation between the agent and external tool services.

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Biomni Agent (A1)"
        A1["A1 Agent"]
        TR["Tool Registry<br/>ToolRegistry"]
        M2A["module2api Mapping"]
        CF["_custom_functions<br/>Dict"]
    end

    subgraph "Inbound MCP: add_mcp()"
        YAML["mcp_config.yaml"]
        DSC["Tool Discovery<br/>async stdio_client"]
        WRAP["Sync Wrapper Factory<br/>make_mcp_wrapper"]
        YAML --> DSC
        DSC --> WRAP
        WRAP --> TR
        WRAP --> M2A
        WRAP --> CF
    end

    subgraph "Outbound MCP: create_mcp_server"
        FMCP["FastMCP Server<br/>'BiomniTools'"]
        WS["_generate_mcp_wrapper<br/>from schema"]
        M2A --> WS
        WS --> FMCP
    end

    subgraph "External MCP Servers"
        GH["GitHub MCP<br/>Docker"]
        PM["PubMed MCP<br/>Python module"]
        CUSTOM["Custom Server<br/>Binary / NPM"]
    end

    A1 -->|"add_mcp(config)"| YAML
    A1 -->|"create_mcp_server(mods)"| FMCP
    DSC <-->|"stdio transport"| GH
    DSC <-->|"stdio transport"| PM
    DSC <-->|"stdio transport"| CUSTOM
    FMCP <-->|"stdio transport"| EXTERNAL_CLIENT["MCP Clients<br/>(Claude, etc.)"]
```

The two integration directions share a common foundation but differ in their data flow. Inbound integration reads a YAML manifest, spawns MCP server processes, discovers their tool schemas, then generates synchronous Python wrappers that are injected into Biomni's tool registry. Outbound integration reverses this: it reads Biomni's internal `module2api` schema, wraps each tool function with proper MCP-compliant parameter annotations, and registers them on a `FastMCP` server instance.

Sources: [a1.py - add_mcp](biomni/agent/a1.py#L350-L410), [a1.py - create_mcp_server](biomni/agent/a1.py#L1995-L2060), [tool_registry.py](biomni/tool/tool_registry.py#L24-L34)

## Integration Mode Comparison

Before diving into implementation details, it helps to understand the structural differences between the two MCP integration patterns. Each serves a distinct workflow and operates under different constraints.

| Aspect | Inbound (`add_mcp`) | Outbound (`create_mcp_server`) |
|---|---|---|
| **Purpose** | Import external tools into Biomni agent | Expose Biomni tools to external MCP clients |
| **Configuration** | YAML file (`mcp_config.yaml`) | Python arguments (`tool_modules` list) |
| **Transport** | stdio client (connects to child processes) | stdio server (listens for client connections) |
| **Schema Source** | MCP server's `inputSchema` or manual YAML definitions | Biomni's `module2api` schema format |
| **Async Handling** | `nest_asyncio` + `asyncio.run()` to bridge sync agent with async MCP | `FastMCP` handles async natively |
| **Registration Target** | `ToolRegistry` + `module2api` + `_custom_functions` | `FastMCP` server object |
| **Tool Discovery** | Automatic (via `list_tools()`) or manual (YAML `tools:` list) | Schema-driven from registered modules |
| **Use After** | Call `agent.go("...")` with MCP tools available | Call `mcp.run(transport="stdio")` to start server |

Sources: [a1.py - add_mcp](biomni/agent/a1.py#L350-L350), [a1.py - create_mcp_server](biomni/agent/a1.py#L1995-L1995), [mcp_integration.md](docs/mcp_integration.md#L7-L10)

## Inbound Integration: Adding External MCP Servers

The inbound integration path lets you bring tools from any MCP-compatible server into Biomni's agent loop. The entry point is the [`add_mcp()`](biomni/agent/a1.py#L350) method on the `A1` agent instance. It accepts a single argument — the path to a YAML configuration file — and handles the entire lifecycle of tool discovery, wrapper generation, and registry insertion.

### Configuration File Format

MCP servers are declared under the top-level `mcp_servers` key in a YAML file. Each server entry requires a `command` array (the process invocation), supports an `enabled` flag, optional `env` variables with `${VAR}` substitution, and either automatic tool discovery or explicit manual tool definitions.

```yaml
mcp_servers:
  # Auto-discovery mode: no 'tools' key → discovers all tools from the server
  github:
    command: ["docker", "run", "-i", "--rm", "-e", "GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN", "ghcr.io/github/github-mcp-server"]
    enabled: true
    env:
      GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN: "${GITHUB_TOKEN}"

  # Manual mode: explicit 'tools' list with Biomni-specific schema
  pubmed:
    command: ["python", "-m", "biomni.tool.example_mcp_tools.pubmed_mcp"]
    enabled: true
    tools:
      - biomni_name: search_pubmed
        description: "Search PubMed"
        parameters:
          query:        {type: str, required: true,  description: "PubMed search term"}
          max_results:  {type: int, required: false, default: 10, description: "Max results"}
      - biomni_name: get_article_abstract
        description: "Fetch PubMed abstract"
        parameters:
          pmid: {type: str, required: true, description: "PubMed ID"}
```

The `command` field follows the same pattern regardless of server packaging type. The table below summarizes the common invocation patterns:

| Server Type | `command` Format | Prerequisites |
|---|---|---|
| **Docker container** | `["docker", "run", "-i", "--rm", ...]` | Docker daemon running |
| **NPM package** | `["npx", "-y", "@scope/server-name"]` | Node.js and npm installed |
| **Python module** | `["python", "-m", "package.module"]` | Package in `PYTHONPATH` |
| **Binary executable** | `["./my-server", "--config", "path"]` | Executable with run permission |

Sources: [mcp_config.yaml](tutorials/examples/add_mcp_server/mcp_config.yaml#L1-L26), [mcp_integration.md](docs/mcp_integration.md#L16-L32)

### The Tool Discovery and Registration Pipeline

When `add_mcp()` is called, it executes a multi-stage pipeline that transforms remote MCP tool definitions into locally callable Python functions integrated into Biomni's tool ecosystem. Understanding this pipeline is essential for debugging and for building custom MCP servers that integrate cleanly.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    START["agent.add_mcp(config_path)"] --> LOAD["Load & parse YAML config"]
    LOAD --> LOOP{For each<br/>enabled server}
    LOOP --> PARSE["Parse command array<br/>cmd, *args = cmd_list"]
    PARSE --> ENV["Process env vars<br/>${VAR} → os.getenv()"]
    ENV --> HAS_TOOLS{"Has explicit<br/>tools: list?"}

    HAS_TOOLS -->|Yes: manual mode| MANUAL["Use YAML tool definitions<br/>biomni_name, parameters"]
    HAS_TOOLS -->|No: auto-discover| SPAWN["Spawn MCP server process<br/>StdioServerParameters"]

    SPAWN --> DISCOVER["Call list_tools() via stdio<br/>async session"]
    DISCOVER --> CHECK{Tools found?}
    CHECK -->|No| WARN["Warning, skip server"] --> LOOP
    CHECK -->|Yes| TOOLS["Extract name, description,<br/>inputSchema per tool"]

    MANUAL --> REG["For each tool:"]
    TOOLS --> REG

    REG --> WRAP["make_mcp_wrapper()<br/>Create sync wrapper function"]
    WRAP --> MOD["Create module namespace<br/>sys.modules['mcp_servers.{name}']"]
    MOD --> SCHEMA["Build tool_schema dict<br/>name, description, params, module, fn"]
    SCHEMA --> REGISTER["tool_registry.register_tool(schema)"]
    REGISTER --> M2API["Add to module2api[mcp_module_name]"]
    M2API --> CUSTOM["_custom_functions[name] = wrapper"]
    CUSTOM --> LOOP

    LOOP -->|All done| CONFIGURE["self.configure()"]
    CONFIGURE --> DONE["MCP tools available<br/>in agent.go() calls"]
```

The critical technical detail is the **async-to-sync bridging**. MCP's `stdio_client` is inherently async, but Biomni's agent executes tools synchronously within its ReAct loop. The [`make_mcp_wrapper()`](biomni/agent/a1.py#L415) function resolves this by creating a closure that spawns a new event loop for each tool invocation via `asyncio.run()`, with `nest_asyncio` applied to the main thread to allow nested loop creation. For each tool call, a fresh `StdioServerParameters` connection is established, the session is initialized, and the tool is invoked with the forwarded keyword arguments.

> [!TIP]
> **Connection lifecycle**: Each MCP tool call creates a **new child process** and establishes a fresh session. There is no persistent connection pooling. This means containerized servers (Docker) will incur startup overhead on every invocation. For latency-sensitive workflows, prefer Python-module-based MCP servers or pre-warmed Docker containers.

Sources: [a1.py - add_mcp](biomni/agent/a1.py#L350-L588), [a1.py - make_mcp_wrapper](biomni/agent/a1.py#L415-L444), [mcp_integration.md](docs/mcp_integration.md#L86-L104)

### Manual vs. Automatic Tool Definitions

The configuration supports two modes for specifying which tools to import, and the difference affects how parameter schemas are interpreted.

**Manual mode** (explicit `tools:` list in YAML): Tool names use the `biomni_name` key. Parameters are defined in Biomni's native schema format — a flat dictionary where each key is a parameter name, and each value is a dict with `type`, `required`, and `description`. The `required` field is per-parameter.

**Auto-discovery mode** (no `tools:` key): The system calls `list_tools()` on the MCP server and reads each tool's `inputSchema` (JSON Schema format). Parameters come from `inputSchema.properties`, and the `required` list lives at the top level of `inputSchema`. Tool names are taken directly from the server's tool `name` attribute.

| Property | Manual Mode | Auto-Discovery Mode |
|---|---|---|
| Tool name source | `biomni_name` key | MCP server's `tool.name` |
| Parameter format | `{name: {type, required, desc}}` | JSON Schema `inputSchema` |
| Required determination | Per-param `required: true` | Top-level `inputSchema.required` array |
| Granularity | Select specific tools | All server tools imported |
| Best for | Large servers where you need a subset | Small, purpose-built servers |

Sources: [a1.py - tool registration](biomni/agent/a1.py#L512-L576), [mcp_config.yaml](tutorials/examples/add_mcp_server/mcp_config.yaml#L12-L25)

### Registration into Biomni's Tool System

Regardless of definition mode, every MCP tool undergoes the same four-part registration. The tool schema is validated by [`ToolRegistry.register_tool()`](biomni/tool/tool_registry.py#L24), which requires `name`, `description`, and `required_parameters` keys. It's then added to the `module2api` dictionary under a synthetic module namespace (`mcp_servers.{server_name}`), stored in the `_custom_functions` instance dict for direct invocation, and finally the agent is re-configured via [`self.configure()`](biomni/agent/a1.py#L1289) to rebuild its system prompt and tool retrieval index with the newly available tools.

Sources: [a1.py - registration](biomni/agent/a1.py#L570-L587), [tool_registry.py](biomni/tool/tool_registry.py#L24-L34)

### Basic Usage Example

```python
from biomni.agent import A1

agent = A1()

# Import MCP servers from a YAML configuration
agent.add_mcp(config_path="./mcp_config.yaml")

# MCP tools are now available in agent queries
result = agent.go("Please list all repositories in the github account of the user.")
```

The configuration file referenced above is provided at [`tutorials/examples/add_mcp_server/mcp_config.yaml`](tutorials/examples/add_mcp_server/mcp_config.yaml#L1-L26) and includes both a GitHub Docker-based server (auto-discovery) and a PubMed Python-based server (manual definitions). The example notebook [`mcp_example.ipynb`](tutorials/examples/add_mcp_server/mcp_example.ipynb#L1-L36) demonstrates end-to-end usage with GitHub token configuration and combined MCP + native tool workflows.

Sources: [mcp_example.ipynb](tutorials/examples/add_mcp_server/mcp_example.ipynb#L1-L36), [mcp_integration.md](docs/mcp_integration.md#L67-L84)

## Building a Custom MCP Server for Biomni

Biomni includes a reference implementation of a custom MCP server at [`biomni/tool/example_mcp_tools/pubmed_mcp.py`](biomni/tool/example_mcp_tools/pubmed_mcp.py#L1-L38). This file demonstrates the minimal pattern for creating a Biomni-consumable MCP server using the `FastMCP` framework.

```python
from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP
from pydantic import BaseModel

mcp = FastMCP("pubmed-live")

class Article(BaseModel):
    pmid: str
    title: str | None = None
    journal: str | None = None

@mcp.tool()
def search_pubmed(query: str, max_results: int = 10) -> list[Article]:
    """Search PubMed for articles matching the query."""
    # ... implementation ...
    return articles

@mcp.tool()
def get_article_abstract(pmid: str) -> str:
    """Fetch the abstract for a given PubMed ID."""
    # ... implementation ...
    return abstract_text

if __name__ == "__main__":
    mcp.run()
```

The key design decisions visible in this reference implementation: `FastMCP` handles the stdio transport and tool registration automatically, Pydantic models provide type-safe structured outputs, and the `@mcp.tool()` decorator exposes functions with their signatures and docstrings as tool schemas. When used with manual mode in the YAML config (as shown in the `pubmed` server definition), the `biomni_name` field maps the MCP tool's internal name to a Biomni-friendly name, while the manual `parameters` block lets you control exactly which parameters are exposed and how they're documented to the agent.

> [!TIP]
> **Parameter naming alignment**: When using manual tool definitions, ensure the `biomni_name` and the `parameters` key names exactly match the MCP server's actual tool name and parameter names. The wrapper generated by `make_mcp_wrapper()` passes keyword arguments directly to `session.call_tool(tool_name, kwargs)`, so a mismatch will result in silent argument dropping or server-side validation errors.

Sources: [pubmed_mcp.py](biomni/tool/example_mcp_tools/pubmed_mcp.py#L1-L38), [a1.py - make_mcp_wrapper](biomni/agent/a1.py#L415-L444)

## Outbound Integration: Exposing Biomni as MCP Server

The reverse integration path — making Biomni's tools available to external MCP clients — is handled by the [`create_mcp_server()`](biomni/agent/a1.py#L1995) method. This creates a `FastMCP` server instance that wraps Biomni's internal tool functions with MCP-compliant signatures, allowing any MCP-compatible client (Claude Desktop, custom agents, etc.) to invoke Biomni tools.

### How Tool Wrapping Works

The [`create_mcp_server()`](biomni/agent/a1.py#L1995) method iterates over the specified tool modules (or all modules in `self.module2api` if none are specified). For each tool schema, it retrieves the actual function from the module, then generates a wrapper via [`_generate_mcp_wrapper_from_biomni_schema()`](biomni/agent/a1.py#L2541). This wrapper performs three critical transformations: it filters incoming `kwargs` to only include declared parameters, it wraps all exceptions into `{"error": str(e)}` response dicts rather than propagating them, and it normalizes non-dict return values into `{"result": value}` envelopes.

The type mapping system converts Biomni's string-based type annotations to Python type objects for proper MCP schema generation:

| Biomni Schema Type | Python Type | MCP JSON Schema |
|---|---|---|
| `str` | `str` | `string` |
| `int` | `int` | `integer` |
| `float` | `float` | `number` |
| `bool` | `bool` | `boolean` |
| `List[str]` | `list[str]` | `array` |
| `dict` | `dict` | `object` |

Required parameters are registered as keyword-only with no default, while optional parameters receive a `None` default with a union type annotation (`T | None`).

Sources: [a1.py - create_mcp_server](biomni/agent/a1.py#L1995-L2060), [a1.py - wrapper generation](biomni/agent/a1.py#L2541-L2625)

### Running the Server

The production-ready server launcher is at [`tutorials/examples/expose_biomni_server/run_mcp_server.py`](tutorials/examples/expose_biomni_server/run_mcp_server.py#L1-L13):

```python
from biomni.agent.a1 import A1

agent = A1()
mcp = agent.create_mcp_server(tool_modules=["biomni.tool.database"])

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("Starting Biomni MCP server...")
    mcp.run(transport="stdio")
```

You can specify any subset of Biomni's tool modules. The `module2api` mapping includes modules like `biomni.tool.genetics`, `biomni.tool.cell_biology`, `biomni.tool.database`, and dozens more. The server logs the total count of registered tools on startup, making it straightforward to verify that the expected tools were loaded.

### Testing the Server

A comprehensive test client is provided at [`test_mcp_server.py`](tutorials/examples/expose_biomni_server/test_mcp_server.py#L1-L174). This script uses the MCP client SDK's `stdio_client` to connect to the server, lists all available tools with their schemas, and invokes a specified tool with test arguments. It includes pre-configured test cases for tools like `query_uniprot`, `blast_sequence`, and `region_to_ccre_screen` that can be activated by uncommenting the relevant configuration block.

```python
# Configuration in test_mcp_server.py
TOOL_TO_TEST = "query_uniprot"
TEST_ARGS = {"prompt": "Find information about human insulin protein"}
```

The test script performs structured output parsing — it attempts JSON deserialization of results and displays them in a readable format with type-aware truncation for large lists and dicts. This makes it invaluable for validating that tool responses conform to expected schemas before integrating with production MCP clients.

Sources: [run_mcp_server.py](tutorials/examples/expose_biomni_server/run_mcp_server.py#L1-L13), [test_mcp_server.py](tutorials/examples/expose_biomni_server/test_mcp_server.py#L1-L174), [mcp_integration.md](docs/mcp_integration.md#L121-L156)

## Environment Variable Substitution

Both integration modes support environment variable injection. In the YAML config, the `${VARIABLE_NAME}` syntax triggers substitution via `os.getenv()` at config-load time [source](biomni/agent/a1.py#L478-L487). The substitution is **not recursive** — only one level of `${...}` is resolved. Static string values are passed through unchanged.

```yaml
env:
  GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN: "${GITHUB_TOKEN}"  # Resolved from environment
  NCBI_EMAIL: "${NCBI_EMAIL}"                      # Resolved from environment
  DEBUG_MODE: "true"                                # Static string, passed as-is
```

For the outbound server, environment variables flow through to child processes via `os.environ.copy()` in the `StdioServerParameters` construction, ensuring that any credentials needed by the underlying Biomni tools (API keys for database queries, etc.) are available to the server process.

> [!TIP]
> **Missing variable behavior**: If a `${VAR}` reference points to an unset environment variable, `os.getenv(var_name, "")` substitutes an empty string. This will not raise an error at config-load time but will likely cause authentication failures at tool-invocation time. Always verify that required environment variables are set before calling `add_mcp()`.

Sources: [a1.py - env processing](biomni/agent/a1.py#L478-L487), [mcp_integration.md](docs/mcp_integration.md#L106-L119)

## Troubleshooting Guide

| Symptom | Likely Cause | Resolution |
|---|---|---|
| `Failed to discover tools` | MCP server process fails to start | Verify the `command` array is correct; check that Docker/Node/Python is available in `PATH` |
| `Warning: No tools discovered from {server}` | Server starts but reports no tools | Test the server manually: run the command and check for stderr output |
| `MCP tool execution failed for '{name}'` | Runtime error in tool invocation | Check environment variables; test the tool directly against the MCP server |
| Tool call succeeds but returns unexpected data | Async-to-sync bridging issue | Verify `nest_asyncio` is installed; check for event loop conflicts in your runtime |
| `Invalid tool format` | Schema validation failure in `ToolRegistry` | Ensure the tool schema has `name`, `description`, and `required_parameters` keys |
| Duplicate tool name warnings | Two servers expose the same tool name | Use manual mode with unique `biomni_name` values to disambiguate |

The `test_mcp_server.py` script provides the most effective diagnostic path for outbound integration issues. For inbound problems, adding `print()` statements inside the `sync_tool_wrapper` closure (in [`make_mcp_wrapper`](biomni/agent/a1.py#L415)) will reveal whether the MCP server process is launching correctly and returning data.

Sources: [mcp_integration.md](docs/mcp_integration.md#L181-L203), [tool_registry.py](biomni/tool/tool_registry.py#L32-L34)


Sources: [pubmed_mcp.py](biomni/tool/example_mcp_tools/pubmed_mcp.py#L1-L38), [mcp_config.yaml](tutorials/examples/add_mcp_server/mcp_config.yaml#L1-L26), [run_mcp_server.py](tutorials/examples/expose_biomni_server/run_mcp_server.py#L1-L13), [test_mcp_server.py](tutorials/examples/expose_biomni_server/test_mcp_server.py#L1-L174)

# Commercial vs Academic Mode



Biomni operates across two distinct licensing regimes that govern which datasets, knowledge resources, and retrieval contexts the agent can access. The mode is not a feature toggle that changes agent behavior — it is a **data governance boundary** that determines which resources are injected into the agent's system prompt, thereby shaping every downstream reasoning and tool-selection decision.

## Architectural Overview

The commercial mode implementation follows a strategy pattern: at agent initialization time, the `A1` constructor selects one of two parallel environment description modules, each containing a pre-filtered `data_lake_dict`. A secondary filter is then applied to the know-how document library. Both mechanisms execute **before** the system prompt is generated, meaning the agent never sees excluded resources and cannot attempt to access them.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Agent Initialization] --> B{commercial_mode?}
    B -->|False| C[Import env_desc.py]
    B -->|True| D[Import env_desc_cm.py]
    C --> E[data_lake_dict<br/>78 datasets]
    D --> F[data_lake_dict<br/>44 datasets<br/>34 excluded]
    E --> G[Know-How Loader]
    F --> G
    G --> H{Filter know-how docs<br/>for commercial restrictions?}
    B -->|True| I[Remove docs with<br/>❌ / Not Allowed / Non-Commercial]
    B -->|False| J[All know-how docs<br/>loaded]
    I --> K[System Prompt Generation]
    J --> K
    E --> K
    F --> K
    K --> L[Agent Ready]
```

Sources: [a1.py](biomni/agent/a1.py#L56-L230), [config.py](biomni/config.py#L12-L68)

## Configuration Methods

There are three equivalent paths to enable commercial mode, each resolved in a strict priority order. The constructor parameter takes precedence over the environment variable, which in turn overrides the `BiomniConfig` default.

| Method | Syntax | Priority | Scope |
|--------|--------|----------|-------|
| **Constructor argument** | `A1(commercial_mode=True)` | Highest (evaluated first) | Per-agent instance |
| **Environment variable** | `BIOMNI_COMMERCIAL_MODE=true` | Medium (overridden by constructor) | Process-wide |
| **Config dataclass** | `BiomniConfig(commercial_mode=True)` | Lowest (fallback default) | Shared across instances |

The `__post_init__` method in `BiomniConfig` reads the environment variable during instantiation ([config.py#L67-L68](biomni/config.py#L67-L68)), but the `A1.__init__` constructor applies its own cascade: any explicitly-passed parameter overrides the `default_config` singleton ([a1.py#L93-L95](biomni/agent/a1.py#L93-L95)). This means setting `commercial_mode=True` on a specific `A1` instance will work regardless of the environment variable state, while leaving the parameter as `None` defers to whatever `BiomniConfig` resolved.

When commercial mode activates, the constructor emits a diagnostic line to stdout:
- Academic mode: `"🎓 Academic mode: Using all datasets (including non-commercial)"`
- Commercial mode: `"🏢 Commercial mode: Using commercial-licensed datasets only"`

Additionally, the configuration block printed at startup displays the resolved mode as either `"Commercial (licensed datasets only)"` or `"Academic (all datasets)"` ([a1.py#L110-L113](biomni/agent/a1.py#L110-L113)).

Sources: [config.py](biomni/config.py#L43-L68), [a1.py](biomni/agent/a1.py#L85-L126)

## Data Lake Exclusions

The data lake is the primary resource affected by mode switching. The academic module [env_desc.py](biomni/env_desc.py) exposes the full catalog of 78 datasets, while the commercial module [env_desc_cm.py](biomni/env_desc_cm.py) comments out 34 entries that carry non-commercial licensing. The software library (`library_content_dict`) is **identical** between both modules — no Python packages, R packages, or CLI tools are excluded regardless of mode.

### Excluded Datasets by License Category

| License Category | Datasets Excluded | Key Affected Domains |
|---|---|---|
| **CC BY-NC-SA 4.0** | DDInter (8 files), DisGeNET, McPAS-TCR | Drug-drug interactions, gene-disease associations, TCR specificity |
| **CC BY-NC 4.0** | miRTarBase (3 files) | Validated microRNA-target interactions |
| **Commercial license required** | MSigDB (10 files), OMIM, BindingDB | Gene set enrichment, genetic disorders, drug-target binding |
| **Proprietary / permission required** | EveBio (7 files), Enamine REAL | Screening assay results, compound libraries |
| **Non-commercial use only** | miRDB | Predicted microRNA targets |

This removes entire analytical domains from the agent's awareness. For example, with MSigDB's 10 gene set collections excluded, the agent loses access to hallmark gene sets, oncogenic signatures, immunologic signatures, and curated positional gene sets — all critical for pathway enrichment analysis. The omission of DDInter's 8 drug-drug interaction files similarly blinds the agent to a comprehensive pharmacovigilance resource.

Sources: [env_desc_cm.py](biomni/env_desc_cm.py#L1-L80), [env_desc.py](biomni/env_desc.py#L1-L80)

### Impact on Downstream Capabilities

The data lake dictionary is not merely a file inventory — each entry includes a human-readable description that is injected verbatim into the system prompt. When a dataset is excluded, its description disappears from the prompt entirely. This means:

1. **The agent cannot discover excluded datasets** through tool retrieval, since the retriever operates over the system prompt's resource catalog.
2. **The agent cannot reference excluded datasets in code**, because the dataset descriptions serve as the agent's primary knowledge about available file paths and their contents.
3. **Query routing is affected**: the agent's `use_tool_retriever` path ([a1.py#L1646-L1655](biomni/agent/a1.py#L1646-L1655)) selects resources from the already-filtered catalog before generating the prompt.

Sources: [a1.py](biomni/agent/a1.py#L898-L940), [a1.py](biomni/agent/a1.py#L1646-L1655)

## Know-How Document Filtering

In addition to the data lake, commercial mode applies a secondary filter to the know-how library — the collection of curated methodology guides and best-practice documents stored as markdown files under `biomni/know_how/`. The `_filter_know_how_for_commercial_mode()` method inspects each document's `commercial_use` metadata field and removes any document containing the markers `❌`, `Not Allowed`, or `Non-Commercial` ([a1.py#L876-L893](biomni/agent/a1.py#L876-L893)).

```python
# Detection logic (simplified)
for doc_id, doc in self.know_how_loader.documents.items():
    commercial_use = metadata.get("commercial_use", "")
    if "❌" in commercial_use or "Not Allowed" in commercial_use or "Non-Commercial" in commercial_use:
        docs_to_remove.append(doc_id)
```

Each know-how document includes a YAML-like metadata section parsed by `KnowHowLoader._extract_metadata()` ([loader.py#L64-L100](biomni/know_how/loader.py#L64-L100)). Documents that permit commercial use mark this explicitly with `**Commercial Use**: ✅ Allowed` (as seen in both [single_cell_annotation.md](biomni/know_how/single_cell_annotation.md#L1-L30) and [sgRNA_design_guide.md](biomni/know_how/sgRNA_design_guide.md#L1-L30)). Documents without any `commercial_use` metadata field are **retained by default** — the filter only acts on explicit prohibitions.

Excluded documents are removed from the in-memory `documents` dictionary via `KnowHowLoader.remove_document()` and cannot be recovered without reloading the entire document set.

> [!TIP]
> The know-how filter is additive: you can add custom know-how documents at runtime via `KnowHowLoader.add_custom_document()` and include a `commercial_use` metadata field to control their visibility under commercial mode. The filtering runs only once during `__init__`, so documents added after construction bypass the filter entirely unless you manually invoke `_filter_know_how_for_commercial_mode()`.

Sources: [a1.py](biomni/agent/a1.py#L876-L893), [loader.py](biomni/know_how/loader.py#L28-L100), [single_cell_annotation.md](biomni/know_how/single_cell_annotation.md#L1-L30)

## What Remains Unchanged

Two resource layers are **not affected** by commercial mode:

1. **Software library** (`library_content_dict`): Both [env_desc.py](biomni/env_desc.py#L81-L222) and [env_desc_cm.py](biomni/env_desc_cm.py#L81-L220) contain identical package and tool inventories. All Python packages (rdkit, scanpy, biopython, etc.), R packages (DESeq2, clusterProfiler, etc.), and CLI tools (samtools, bedtools, etc.) remain available in both modes.

2. **Custom resources**: Any tools, data, or software added at runtime via `A1.add_tool()`, `A1.add_data()`, or `A1.add_software()` are not subject to mode filtering. These custom entries are maintained in separate dictionaries and appended to the system prompt independently ([a1.py#L676-L786](biomni/agent/a1.py#L676-L786)).

This design is intentional: the software tools themselves carry compatible open-source licenses, while the licensing restrictions apply to the **data** those tools operate on and the **knowledge** resources that guide their use.

Sources: [env_desc_cm.py](biomni/env_desc_cm.py#L81-L220), [a1.py](biomni/agent/a1.py#L676-L860)

## Practical Guidance

### When to Use Academic Mode

Academic mode (`commercial_mode=False`, the default) provides maximum analytical breadth. Use it for research, exploratory analysis, and any work that falls squarely under non-commercial or academic licensing terms. The additional 34 datasets significantly expand the agent's ability to perform drug repurposing analysis, gene set enrichment, miRNA target prediction, and drug-drug interaction checks.

### When to Use Commercial Mode

Commercial mode (`commercial_mode=True`) should be activated for any deployment where results may be used in a commercial context — pharmaceutical R&D at for-profit entities, contract research, or commercial product development. It provides a compliance boundary by construction: the agent physically cannot access excluded resources, eliminating the risk of inadvertent licensing violations in generated code or analysis outputs.

### Mode Selection Decision Flow

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Deployment Context?] --> B{For-profit<br/>entity or<br/>commercial product?}
    B -->|Yes| C[commercial_mode=True]
    B -->|No| D{Published research<br/>or internal<br/>academic use?}
    D -->|Yes| E[commercial_mode=False<br/>Academic mode]
    D -->|Uncertain| F[commercial_mode=True<br/>Conservative default]
    C --> G[Verify: custom data<br/>licenses separately]
    E --> G
    F --> G
```

Sources: [config.py](biomni/config.py#L43-L43), [a1.py](biomni/agent/a1.py#L95-L102)

### Runtime Verification

After agent instantiation, you can verify the active mode by inspecting the `commercial_mode` attribute or checking the size of the loaded resource catalogs:

```python
agent = A1(commercial_mode=True)
print(agent.commercial_mode)               # True
print(len(agent.data_lake_dict))           # ~44 (vs ~78 in academic mode)
print(len(agent.know_how_loader.documents)) # Reduced if non-commercial docs exist
```

The agent prints a full configuration summary at startup, including the resolved mode and data statistics ([a1.py#L108-L126](biomni/agent/a1.py#L108-L126)).
